{{short description|Equalities for combinations of sets}}

This article lists [[Mathematics|mathematical]] properties and laws of [[Set (mathematics)|sets]], involving the set-theoretic [[Operation (mathematics)|operations]] of [[Union (set theory)|union]], [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]], and [[Complement (set theory)|complementation]] and the [[Binary relation|relations]] of set [[Equality (mathematics)|equality]] and set [[Subset|inclusion]]. It also provides systematic procedures for evaluating expressions, and performing calculations, involving these operations and relations.

The [[binary operation]]s of set union (<math>\cup</math>) and intersection (<math>\cap</math>) satisfy many identities. Several of these identities or "laws" have well established names. 

==Notation==

Throughout this article, capital letters (such as <math>A, B, C, L, M, R, S,</math> and <math>X</math>) will denote sets. On the left hand side of an identity,
* <math>L</math> will be the <math>L</math>{{hsp}}eft most set, 
* <math>M</math> will be the <math>M</math>{{hsp}}iddle set, and 
* <math>R</math> will be the <math>R</math>{{hsp}}ight most set.
This is to facilitate applying identities to expressions that are complicated or use the same symbols as the identity.<ref group=note>
For example, the expression <math>(M \setminus R) \setminus A</math> uses two of the same symbols (<math>M</math> and <math>R</math>) that appear in the identity 
<math display=block>(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\setminus\, R ~=~ (L \,\setminus\, R) \,\setminus\, (M \,\setminus\, R)</math>
but they refer to different sets in each expression. 
To apply this identity to <math>(M \setminus R) \setminus A,</math> substitute <math>\text{Left set} := M,\;</math> <math>\text{Middle set} := R,\;</math> and <math>\text{Right set} := A</math> (since these are the left, middle, and right sets in <math>(M \setminus R) \setminus A</math>) to obtain: 
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
(M \setminus R) \setminus A 
&= (\text{Left set } &&\setminus \text{Right set}&&) &&\setminus (\text{Middle set } &&\setminus \text{Right set}) \\
&= (M &&\setminus A&&) &&\setminus (R &&\setminus A). \\
\end{alignat}</math>
For a second example, this time applying the identity to <math>((M \cap R \setminus L) \setminus (A \triangle L)) \setminus L,</math> is now given. The identity <math display=inline>(L \setminus M) \setminus R = (L \setminus R) \setminus (M \setminus R)</math> can be applied to <math>((M \cap R \setminus L) \setminus (A \triangle L)) \setminus L</math> by reading <math>L, M,</math> and <math>R</math> as <math>\text{Left}, \text{Middle},</math> and <math>\text{Right}</math> and then substituting <math>\text{Left} = (M \cap R \setminus L),</math> <math>\text{Middle} = (A \triangle L),</math> and <math>\text{Right} = L</math> to obtain:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
((M \cap R \setminus L) \setminus (A \triangle L)) \setminus L 
&= (\text{Left } &&\setminus \text{Right}&&) &&\setminus (\text{Middle } &&\setminus \text{Right}) \\
&= ((M \cap R \setminus L) &&\setminus L&&) &&\setminus ((A \triangle L) &&\setminus L). \\
\end{alignat}</math>
</ref> 
For example, the identity 
<math display=block>(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\setminus\, R ~=~ (L \,\setminus\, R) \,\setminus\, (M \,\setminus\, R)</math>
may be read as:
<math display=block>(\text{Left set} \,\setminus\, \text{Middle set}) \,\setminus\, \text{Right set} ~=~ (\text{Left set} \,\setminus\, \text{Right set}) \,\setminus\, (\text{Middle set} \,\setminus\, \text{Right set}).</math>

===Elementary set operations===

For sets <math>L</math> and <math>R,</math> define:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
L \cup R      &&~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{~ x ~:~ x \in L \;&&\text{ or }\;\, &&\; x \in R ~\} \\
L \cap R      &&~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{~ x ~:~ x \in L \;&&\text{ and }    &&\; x \in R ~\} \\
L \setminus R &&~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{~ x ~:~ x \in L \;&&\text{ and }    &&\; x \notin R ~\} \\
\end{alignat}</math>
and
<math display=block>L \triangle R ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{~ x ~:~ x \text{ belongs to exactly one of } L \text{ and } R ~\}</math>
where the {{em|[[symmetric difference]]}} <math>L \triangle R</math> is sometimes denoted by <math>L \ominus R</math> and equals:<ref name="Taylor 2019">{{Cite web|last=Taylor|first=Courtney|date=March 31, 2019|title=What Is Symmetric Difference in Math?|url=https://www.thoughtco.com/what-is-the-symmetric-difference-3126594|access-date=2020-09-05|website=ThoughtCo|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Weisstein 2020">{{Cite web|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|title=Symmetric Difference|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SymmetricDifference.html|access-date=2020-09-05|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en}}</ref>
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
L \;\triangle\; R 
~&=~ (L ~\setminus~ &&R) ~\cup~      &&(R ~\setminus~ &&L) \\
~&=~ (L ~\cup~      &&R) ~\setminus~ &&(L ~\cap~      &&R). 
\end{alignat}</math>

One set <math>L</math> is said to {{em|intersect}} another set <math>R</math> if <math>L \cap R \neq \varnothing.</math> Sets that do not intersect are said to be {{em|[[Disjoint sets|disjoint]]}}. 

The [[power set]] of <math>X</math> is the set of all subsets of <math>X</math> and will be denoted by
<math display=block>\mathcal{P}(X) ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{~ L ~:~ L \subseteq X ~\}.</math>

'''Universe set and complement notation'''

The notation 
<math display=block>L^\complement ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ X \setminus L.</math>
may be used if <math>L</math> is a subset of some set <math>X</math> that is understood (say from context, or because it is clearly stated what the superset <math>X</math> is). 
It is emphasized that the definition of <math>L^\complement</math> depends on context. For instance, had <math>L</math> been declared as a subset of <math>Y,</math> with the sets <math>Y</math> and <math>X</math> not necessarily related to each other in any way, then <math>L^\complement</math> would likely mean <math>Y \setminus L</math> instead of <math>X \setminus L.</math>

If it is needed then unless indicated otherwise, it should be assumed that <math>X</math> denotes the [[Universe (mathematics)|universe set]], which means that all sets that are used in the formula are subsets of <math>X.</math> 
In particular, the [[Complement (set theory)|complement of a set]] <math>L</math> will be denoted by <math>L^\complement</math> where unless indicated otherwise, it should be assumed that <math>L^\complement</math> denotes the complement of <math>L</math> in (the universe) <math>X.</math>

==One subset involved==

Assume <math>L \subseteq X.</math>

'''[[Identity element|Identity]]''':{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}

'''Definition''': <math>e</math> is called a '''[[left identity element]]''' of a [[binary operator]] <math>\,\ast\,</math> if <math>e \,\ast\, R = R</math> for all <math>R</math> and it is called a '''[[right identity element]]''' of <math>\,\ast\,</math> if <math>L \,\ast\, e = L</math> for all <math>L.</math> A left identity element that is also a right identity element if called an '''[[identity element]]'''.

The empty set <math>\varnothing</math> is an identity element of binary union <math>\cup</math> and symmetric difference <math>\triangle,</math> and it is also a right identity element of set subtraction <math>\, \setminus:</math> 

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{10}
L \cap X                  &\;=\;&& L &\;=\;&  X \cap L                  ~~~~\text{ where } L \subseteq X \\[1.4ex]
L \cup \varnothing        &\;=\;&& L &\;=\;& \varnothing \cup L        \\[1.4ex]
L \,\triangle \varnothing &\;=\;&& L &\;=\;& \varnothing \,\triangle L \\[1.4ex]
L \setminus \varnothing   &\;=\;&& L \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
but <math>\varnothing</math> is not a left identity element of <math>\, \setminus \,</math> since
<math display=block>\varnothing \setminus L = \varnothing</math> 
so <math display=inline>\varnothing \setminus L = L</math> if and only if <math>L = \varnothing.</math>

'''[[Idempotent|Idempotence]]'''{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}} <math>L \ast L = L</math> and '''[[Nilpotent|Nilpotence]]''' <math>L \ast L = \varnothing</math>:

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{10}
L \cup L                  &\;=\;&& L            && \quad \text{ (Idempotence)} \\[1.4ex]
L \cap L                  &\;=\;&& L            && \quad \text{ (Idempotence)} \\[1.4ex]
L \,\triangle\, L         &\;=\;&& \varnothing  && \quad \text{ (Nilpotence of index 2)} \\[1.4ex]
L \setminus L             &\;=\;&& \varnothing  && \quad \text{ (Nilpotence of index 2)} \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

'''Domination'''{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}/[[Absorbing element]]:

'''Definition''': <math>z</math> is called a '''[[left absorbing element]]''' of a [[binary operator]] <math>\,\ast\,</math> if <math>z \,\ast\, R = z</math> for all <math>R</math> and it is called a '''[[right absorbing element]]''' of <math>\,\ast\,</math> if <math>L \,\ast\, z = z</math> for all <math>L.</math> A left absorbing element that is also a right absorbing element is called an '''[[absorbing element]]'''. Absorbing elements are also sometime called '''annihilating elements''' or '''zero elements'''.

A universe set is an absorbing element of binary union <math>\cup.</math> The empty set <math>\varnothing</math> is an absorbing element of binary intersection <math>\cap</math> and binary Cartesian product <math>\times,</math> and it is also a left absorbing element of set subtraction <math>\, \setminus:</math> 

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{10}
X \cup L                  &\;=\;&& X           &\;=\;& L \cup X ~~~~\text{ where } L \subseteq X \\[1.4ex]
\varnothing \cap L        &\;=\;&& \varnothing &\;=\;& L \cap \varnothing  \\[1.4ex]
\varnothing \times L      &\;=\;&& \varnothing &\;=\;& L \times \varnothing \\[1.4ex]
\varnothing \setminus L   &\;=\;&& \varnothing &\;\;& \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
but <math>\varnothing</math> is not a right absorbing element of set subtraction since
<math display=block>L \setminus \varnothing = L</math> 
where <math display=inline>L \setminus \varnothing = \varnothing</math> if and only if <math display=inline>L = \varnothing.</math>

'''Double complement''' or '''[[Involution (mathematics)|involution]] law''':

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{10}
X \setminus (X \setminus L)
&= L
&&\qquad\text{ Also written }\quad
&&\left(L^\complement\right)^\complement = L
&&\quad&&\text{ where } L \subseteq X \quad
\text{ (Double complement/Involution law)} \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>L \setminus \varnothing = L</math>
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
\varnothing 
&= L           &&\setminus L \\
&= \varnothing &&\setminus L \\
&= L           &&\setminus X ~~~~\text{ where } L \subseteq X \\
\end{alignat}</math>{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}

<math display=block>L^\complement = X \setminus L \quad \text{ (definition of notation)}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{10}
L \,\cup (X \setminus L)
&= X
&&\qquad\text{ Also written }\quad
&&L \cup L^\complement = X
&&\quad&&\text{ where } L \subseteq X
\\[1.4ex]

L \,\triangle (X \setminus L)
&= X
&&\qquad\text{ Also written }\quad
&&L \,\triangle L^\complement = X
&&\quad&&\text{ where } L \subseteq X
\\[1.4ex]

L \,\cap (X \setminus L)
&= \varnothing
&&\qquad\text{ Also written }\quad
&&L \cap L^\complement = \varnothing
&&\quad&&
\\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{10}
X \setminus \varnothing
&= X
&&\qquad\text{ Also written }\quad
&&\varnothing^\complement = X
&&\quad&&\text{ (Complement laws for the empty set))}
\\[1.4ex]

X \setminus X
&= \varnothing
&&\qquad\text{ Also written }\quad
&&X^\complement = \varnothing
&&\quad&&\text{ (Complement laws for the universe set)}
\\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

==Two sets involved==

In the left hand sides of the following identities, <math>L</math> is the {{em|L}}{{hsp}}eft most set and <math>R</math> is the {{em|R}}{{hsp}}ight most set. 
Assume both <math>L \text{ and } R</math> are subsets of some universe set <math>X.</math>

===Formulas for binary set operations {{math|⋂, ⋃, \}}, and {{math|∆}}===

In the left hand sides of the following identities, {{mvar|L}} is the {{em|L}}{{hsp}}eft most set and {{mvar|R}} is the {{em|R}}{{hsp}}ight most set. Whenever necessary, both {{mvar|L}} and {{mvar|R}} should be assumed to be subsets of some universe set {{mvar|X}}, so that <math>L^\complement := X \setminus L \text{ and } R^\complement := X \setminus R.</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
L \cap R
&= L &&\,\,\setminus\,   &&(L &&\,\,\setminus &&R) \\
&= R &&\,\,\setminus\,   &&(R &&\,\,\setminus &&L) \\
&= L &&\,\,\setminus\,   &&(L &&\,\triangle\, &&R) \\
&= L &&\,\triangle\,     &&(L &&\,\,\setminus &&R) \\
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
L \cup R
&= (&&L \,\triangle\, R) &&\,\,\cup      && &&L &&       &&  \\
&= (&&L \,\triangle\, R) &&\,\triangle\, &&(&&L &&\cap\, &&R) \\
&= (&&R \,\setminus\, L) &&\,\,\cup      && &&L &&       &&    ~~~~~\text{ (union is disjoint)} \\
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
L \,\triangle\, R
&=  &&R \,\triangle\, L    &&                  && &&                     && \\
&= (&&L \,\cup\, R)        &&\,\setminus\,     &&(&&L \,\,\cap\, R)      && \\
&= (&&L \,\setminus\, R)   &&\cup\,            &&(&&R \,\,\setminus\, L) && ~~~~~\text{ (union is disjoint)} \\
&= (&&L \,\triangle\, M)   &&\,\triangle\,     &&(&&M \,\triangle\, R)   && ~~~~~\text{ where } M \text{ is an arbitrary set. } \\
&= (&&L^\complement)                 &&\,\triangle\,     &&(&&R^\complement)                 && \\
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
L \setminus R
&=   &&L                   &&\,\,\setminus     &&(L &&\,\,\cap       &&R) \\
&=   &&L                   &&\,\,\cap          &&(L &&\,\triangle\,  &&R) \\
&=   &&L                   &&\,\triangle\,     &&(L &&\,\,\cap       &&R) \\
&=   &&R                   &&\,\triangle\,     &&(L &&\,\,\cup       &&R) \\
\end{alignat}</math>

===De Morgan's laws===

'''[[De Morgan's laws]]''' are the identities:

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{10}
X \setminus (L \cap R)
&= (X \setminus L) \cup (X \setminus R)
&&\quad&&\text{ (De Morgan's law)}
\\[1.4ex]

X \setminus (L \cup R)
&= (X \setminus L) \cap (X \setminus R)
&&\quad&&\text{ (De Morgan's law)}
\\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

where typically <math>L, R \subseteq X</math> (although this assumption <math>L, R \subseteq X</math> is unnecessary, as the identities hold for arbitrary sets <math>L, R, X</math>), in which case they can be rewritten

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
(L \cap R)^\complement = L^\complement \cup R^\complement
&&\quad&&\text{ (De Morgan's law)}
\\[1.4ex]

(L \cup R)^\complement = L^\complement \cap R^\complement
&&\quad&&\text{ (De Morgan's law)}
\\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

When an intersection <math>\cap</math> is on one side then there is a union <math>\cup</math> on the other.  Were there an intersection <math>\cap</math> on both sides then it would instead be the formula for the [[distributive property|left distributivity]] of set subtraction over intersections, which [[#Distributivity_and_set_subtraction_\|does not hold in general]].

===Commutativity===

Unions, intersection, and symmetric difference are '''[[commutative operation]]s''':{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{10}
L \cup R                &\;=\;&& R \cup L        && \quad \text{ (Commutativity)} \\[1.4ex]
L \cap R                &\;=\;&& R \cap L        && \quad \text{ (Commutativity)} \\[1.4ex]
L \,\triangle R         &\;=\;&& R \,\triangle L && \quad \text{ (Commutativity)} \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

Set subtraction is not commutative. However, the commutativity of set subtraction can be characterized: from <math>(L \,\setminus\, R) \cap (R \,\setminus\, L) = \varnothing</math> it follows that:
<math display=block>L \,\setminus\, R = R \,\setminus\, L \quad \text{ if and only if } \quad L = R.</math> 
Said differently, if distinct symbols always represented distinct sets, then the {{em|only}} true formulas of the form <math>\,\cdot\, \,\setminus\, \,\cdot\, = \,\cdot\, \,\setminus\, \,\cdot\,</math> that could be written would be those involving a single symbol; that is, those of the form: <math>S \,\setminus\, S = S \,\setminus\, S.</math> 
But such formulas are necessarily true for {{em|every}} binary operation <math>\,\ast\,</math> (because <math>x \,\ast\, x = x \,\ast\, x</math> must hold by definition of [[Equality (mathematics)|equality]]), and so in this sense, set subtraction is as diametrically opposite to being commutative as is possible for a binary operation. 
Set subtraction is also neither [[left alternative]] nor [[right alternative]]; instead, <math>(L \setminus L) \setminus R = L \setminus (L \setminus R)</math> if and only if <math>L \cap R = \varnothing</math> if and only if <math>(R \setminus L) \setminus L = R \setminus (L \setminus L).</math> 
Set subtraction is [[quasi-commutative]] and satisfies the [[Jordan identity]].

===Other identities involving two sets===

'''[[Absorption law]]s''':

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
L \cup (L \cap R)  &\;=\;&& L  && \quad \text{ (Absorption)} \\[1.4ex]
L \cap (L \cup R)  &\;=\;&& L  && \quad \text{ (Absorption)} \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

'''Other properties'''

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{10}
L \setminus R
&= L \cap (X \setminus R)
&&\qquad\text{ Also written }\quad
&&L \setminus R = L \cap R^\complement
&&\quad&&\text{ where } L, R \subseteq X
\\[1.4ex]

X \setminus (L \setminus R)
&= (X \setminus L) \cup R
&&\qquad\text{ Also written }\quad
&&(L \setminus R)^\complement = L^\complement \cup R
&&\quad&&\text{ where } R \subseteq X
\\[1.4ex]

L \setminus R
&= (X \setminus R) \setminus (X \setminus L)
&&\qquad\text{ Also written }\quad
&&L \setminus R = R^\complement \setminus L^\complement
&&\quad&&\text{ where } L, R \subseteq X
\\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

'''Intervals''':

<math display=block>(a, b) \cap (c, d) = (\max\{a,c\}, \min\{b,d\})</math>
<math display=block>[a, b) \cap [c, d) = [\max\{a,c\}, \min\{b,d\})</math>

===Subsets ⊆ and supersets ⊇===

The following statements are equivalent for any <math>L, R \subseteq X:</math>{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}
<ol>
<li><math>L \subseteq R</math>
* Definition of {{em|[[subset]]}}: if <math>l \in L</math> then <math>l \in R</math></li>
<li></li>
<li><math>L \cap R = L</math></li>
<li><math>L \cup R = R</math></li>
<li><math>L \,\triangle\, R = R \setminus L</math></li>
<li><math>L \,\triangle\, R \subseteq R \setminus L</math></li>
<li><math>L \setminus R = \varnothing</math></li>
<li><math>L</math> and <math>X \setminus R</math> are disjoint (that is, <math>L \cap (X \setminus R) = \varnothing</math>)</li>
<li><math>X \setminus R \subseteq X \setminus L \qquad</math> (that is, <math>R^\complement \subseteq L^\complement</math>)</li>
</ol>

The following statements are equivalent for any <math>L, R \subseteq X:</math>
<ol>
<li><math>L \not\subseteq R</math></li>
<li>There exists some <math>l \in L \setminus R.</math></li>
</ol>

====Set equality====
{{See also|Extensionality}}

The following statements are equivalent:
<ol>
<li><math>L = R</math></li>
<li><math>L \,\triangle\, R = \varnothing</math></li>
<li><math>L \,\setminus\, R = R \,\setminus\, L</math></li>
</ol>

<ul>
<li>If <math>L \cap R = \varnothing</math> then <math>L = R</math> if and only if <math>L = \varnothing = R.</math></li>
<li>'''Uniqueness of complements''': If <math display=inline>L \cup R = X \text{ and } L \cap R = \varnothing</math> then <math>R = X \setminus L</math></li>
</ul>

=====Empty set=====

A set <math>L</math> is '''[[Axiom of empty set|empty]]''' if the sentence <math>\forall x (x \not\in L)</math> is true, where the notation <math>x \not\in L</math> is shorthand for <math>\lnot (x \in L).</math> 

If <math>L</math> is any set then the following are equivalent:
<ol>
<li><math>L</math> is not empty, meaning that the sentence <math>\lnot [\forall x (x \not\in L)]</math> is true (literally, the [[logical negation]] of "<math>L</math> is empty" holds true).</li>
<li>(In [[Constructivism (philosophy of mathematics)|classical mathematics]]) <math>L</math> is [[Inhabited set|inhabited]], meaning: <math>\exists x (x \in L)</math>
* In [[constructive mathematics]], "not empty" and "inhabited" are not equivalent: every inhabited set is not empty but the converse is not always guaranteed; that is, in constructive mathematics, a set <math>L</math> that is not empty (where by definition, "<math>L</math> is empty" means that the statement <math>\forall x (x \not\in L)</math> is true) might not have an [[:wiktionary:inhabitant#English|inhabitant]] (which is an <math>x</math> such that <math>x \in L</math>).
</li>
<li><math>L \not\subseteq R</math> for some set <math>R</math></li>
</ol>

If <math>L</math> is any set then the following are equivalent:
<ol>
<li><math>L</math> is empty (<math>L = \varnothing</math>), meaning: <math>\forall x (x \not\in L)</math></li>
<li><math>L \cup R \subseteq R</math> for every set <math>R</math></li>
<li><math>L \subseteq R</math> for every set <math>R</math></li>
<li><math>L \subseteq R \setminus L</math> for some/every set <math>R</math></li>
<li><math>\varnothing / L = L</math></li>
</ol>

Given any <math>x,</math> the following are equivalent:

<ol>
<li><math display=inline>x \not\in L \setminus R</math></li>
<li><math display=inline>x \in L \cap R \; \text{ or } \; x \not\in L.</math></li>
<li><math display=inline>x \in R \; \text{ or } \; x \not\in L.</math></li>
</ol>

Moreover,
<math display=block>(L \setminus R) \cap R = \varnothing \qquad \text{ always holds}.</math>

====Meets, Joins, and lattice properties====

'''Inclusion is a [[partial order]]''': 
Explicitly, this means that [[Subset|inclusion]] <math>\,\subseteq,\,</math> which is a [[binary operation]], has the following three properties:{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}
<ul>
<li>'''[[Reflexive relation|Reflexivity]]''': 
<math display=inline>L \subseteq L</math></li>
<li>'''[[Antisymmetric relation|Antisymmetry]]''': 
<math display=inline>(L \subseteq R \text{ and } R \subseteq L) \text{ if and only if } L = R</math></li>
<li>'''[[Transitive relation|Transitivity]]''': 
<math display=inline>\text{If }L \subseteq M \text{ and } M \subseteq R \text{ then } L \subseteq R</math></li>
</ul>

The following proposition says that for any set <math>S,</math> the [[power set]] of <math>S,</math> ordered by inclusion, is a [[Lattice (order)|bounded lattice]], and hence together with the distributive and complement laws above, show that it is a [[Boolean algebra (structure)|Boolean algebra]].

'''Existence of a [[least element]] and a [[greatest element]]''': 
<math display=block>\varnothing \subseteq L \subseteq X</math>

'''[[Join (mathematics)|Joins]]/supremums exist''':{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}} 
<math display=block>L \subseteq L \cup R</math>

The union <math>L \cup R</math> is the join/supremum of <math>L</math> and <math>R</math> with respect to <math>\,\subseteq\,</math> because:
<ol>
<li><math>L \subseteq L \cup R</math> and <math>R \subseteq L \cup R,</math> and</li>
<li>if <math>Z</math> is a set such that <math>L \subseteq Z</math> and <math>R \subseteq Z</math> then <math>L \cup R \subseteq Z.</math></li>
</ol>

The intersection <math>L \cap R</math> is the join/supremum of <math>L</math> and <math>R</math> with respect to <math>\,\supseteq.\,</math>

'''[[Meet (mathematics)|Meets]]/infimums exist''':{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}} 
<math display=block>L \cap R \subseteq L</math>

The intersection <math>L \cap R</math> is the meet/infimum of <math>L</math> and <math>R</math> with respect to <math>\,\subseteq\,</math> because:
<ol>
<li>if <math>L \cap R \subseteq L</math> and <math>L \cap R \subseteq R,</math> and</li>
<li>if <math>Z</math> is a set such that <math>Z \subseteq L</math> and <math>Z \subseteq R</math> then <math>Z \subseteq L \cap R.</math></li>
</ol>

The union <math>L \cup R</math> is the meet/infimum of <math>L</math> and <math>R</math> with respect to <math>\,\supseteq.\,</math>

'''Other inclusion properties''':

<math display=block>L \setminus R \subseteq L</math>
<math display=block>(L \setminus R) \cap L = L \setminus R</math>

<ul>
<li>If <math>L \subseteq R</math> then <math>L \,\triangle\, R = R \setminus L.</math></li>
<li>If <math>L \subseteq X</math> and <math>R \subseteq Y</math> then <math>L \times R \subseteq X \times Y</math>{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}</li>
</ul>

==Three sets involved==

In the left hand sides of the following identities, <math>L</math> is the {{em|L}}{{hsp}}eft most set, <math>M</math> is the {{em|M}}{{hsp}}iddle set, and <math>R</math> is the {{em|R}}{{hsp}}ight most set. 

===Precedence rules===

There is no universal agreement on the [[Precedence rule|order of precedence]] of the basic set operators.
Nevertheless, many authors use [[precedence rule]]s for set operators, although these rules vary with the author. 

One common convention is to associate intersection <math>L \cap R = \{x : (x \in L) \land (x \in R)\}</math> with [[Logical conjunction|logical conjunction (and)]] <math>L \land R</math> and associate union <math>L \cup R = \{x : (x \in L) \lor (x \in R)\}</math> with [[Logical disjunction|logical disjunction (or)]] <math>L \lor R,</math> and then transfer the [[Logical connective#Order of precedence|precedence of these logical operator]]s (where <math>\,\land\,</math> has precedence over <math>\,\lor\,</math>) to these set operators, thereby giving <math>\,\cap\,</math> precedence over <math>\,\cup.\,</math> 
So for example, <math>L \cup M \cap R</math> would mean <math>L \cup (M \cap R)</math> since it would be associated with the logical statement <math>L \lor M \land R ~=~ L \lor (M \land R)</math> and similarly, <math>L \cup M \cap R \cup Z</math> would mean <math>L \cup (M \cap R) \cup Z</math> since it would be associated with <math>L \lor M \land R \lor Z ~=~ L \lor (M \land R) \lor Z.</math> 

Sometimes, set complement (subtraction) <math>\,\setminus\,</math> is also associated with [[Logical complement|logical complement (not)]] <math>\,\lnot,\,</math> in which case it will have the highest precedence. 
More specifically, <math>L \setminus R = \{x : (x \in L) \land \lnot (x \in R)\}</math> is rewritten <math>L \land \lnot R</math> so that for example, <math>L \cup M \setminus R</math> would mean <math>L \cup (M \setminus R)</math> since it would be rewritten as the logical statement <math>L \lor M \land \lnot R</math> which is equal to <math>L \lor (M \land \lnot R).</math>
For another example, because <math>L \land \lnot M \land R</math> means <math>L \land (\lnot M) \land R,</math> which is equal to both <math>(L \land (\lnot M)) \land R</math> and <math>L \land ((\lnot M) \land R) ~=~ L \land (R \land (\lnot M))</math> (where <math>(\lnot M) \land R</math> was rewritten as <math>R \land (\lnot M)</math>), the formula <math>L \setminus M \cap R</math> would refer to the set <math>(L \setminus M) \cap R = L \cap (R \setminus M);</math> 
moreover, since <math>L \land (\lnot M) \land R = (L \land R) \land \lnot M,</math> this set is also equal to <math>(L \cap R) \setminus M</math> (other set identities can similarly be deduced from [[propositional calculus]] [[Logical equivalence|identities]] in this way).
However, because set subtraction is not associative <math>(L \setminus M) \setminus R \neq L \setminus (M \setminus R),</math> a formula such as <math>L \setminus M \setminus R</math> would be ambiguous; for this reason, among others, set subtraction is often not assigned any precedence at all. 

[[Symmetric difference]] <math>L \triangle R = \{x : (x \in L) \oplus (x \in R)\}</math> is sometimes associated with [[Exclusive or|exclusive or (xor)]] <math>L \oplus R</math> (also sometimes denoted by <math>\,\veebar</math>), in which case if the order of precedence from highest to lowest is <math>\,\lnot, \,\oplus, \,\land, \,\lor\,</math> then the order of precedence (from highest to lowest) for the set operators would be <math>\,\setminus,\, \triangle,\, \cap,\, \cup.</math> 
There is no universal agreement on the precedence of exclusive disjunction <math>\,\oplus\,</math> with respect to the other logical connectives, which is why symmetric difference <math>\,\triangle\,</math> is not often assigned a precedence.

===Associativity===

'''Definition''': A [[binary operator]] <math>\,\ast\,</math> is called '''[[Associativity|associative]]''' if <math>(L \,\ast\, M) \,\ast\, R = L \,\ast\, (M \,\ast\, R)</math> always holds. 

The following set operators are associative:{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
(L \cup M) \cup R               &\;=\;\;&& L \cup (M \cup R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \cap M) \cap R               &\;=\;\;&& L \cap (M \cap R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle M) \,\triangle R &\;=\;\;&& L \,\triangle (M \,\triangle R) \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

For set subtraction, instead of associativity, only the following is always guaranteed:
<math display=block>(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\setminus\, R \;~~{\color{red}{\subseteq}}~~\; L \,\setminus\, (M \,\setminus\, R)</math>
where equality holds if and only if <math>L \cap R = \varnothing</math> (this condition does not depend on <math>M</math>). Thus 
<math display=inline>\; (L \setminus M) \setminus R = L \setminus (M \setminus R) \;</math> if and only if <math>\; (R \setminus M) \setminus L = R \setminus (M \setminus L), \;</math> 
where the only difference between the left and right hand side set equalities is that the locations of <math>L \text{ and } R</math> have been swapped.

===Distributivity===

'''Definition''': If <math>\ast \text{ and } \bullet</math> are [[binary operator]]s then {{em|<math>\,\ast\,</math> [[Distributivity|'''left distributes''' over]] <math>\,\bullet\,</math>}} if <math display=block>L \,\ast\, (M \,\bullet\, R) ~=~ (L \,\ast\, M) \,\bullet\, (L \,\ast\,R) \qquad\qquad \text{ for all } L, M, R</math>
while {{em|<math>\,\ast\,</math> [[Distributivity|'''right distributes''' over]] <math>\,\bullet\,</math>}} if <math display=block>(L \,\bullet\, M) \,\ast\, R ~=~ (L \,\ast\, R) \,\bullet\, (M \,\ast\,R) \qquad\qquad \text{ for all } L, M, R.</math> 
The operator {{em|<math>\,\ast\,</math> [[Distributivity|'''distributes''' over]] <math>\,\bullet\,</math>}} if it both left distributes and right distributes over <math>\,\bullet\,.\,</math> 
In the definitions above, to transform one side to the other, the innermost operator (the operator inside the parentheses) becomes the outermost operator and the outermost operator becomes the innermost operator.

'''[[Right distributivity]]''':{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
(L \,\cap\, M) \,\cup\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\cup\, R) \,&&\cap\, &&(M \,\cup\, R)             \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\cup\, \text{ over } \,\cap\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\cup\, M) \,\cup\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\cup\, R) \,&&\cup\, &&(M \,\cup\, R)             \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\cup\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\cup\, M) \,\cap\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\cap\, R) \,&&\cup\, &&(M \,\cap\, R)             \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\cap\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\cap\, M) \,\cap\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\cap\, R) \,&&\cap\, &&(M \,\cap\, R)             \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\cap\, \text{ over } \,\cap\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M) \,\cap\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\cap\, R) \,&&\triangle\, &&(M \,\cap\, R)    \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\cap\, \text{ over } \,\triangle\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\cap\, M) \,\times\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\times\, R) \,&&\cap\, &&(M \,\times\, R)             \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\cap\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\cup\, M) \,\times\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\times\, R) \,&&\cup\, &&(M \,\times\, R)              \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\times\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\times\, R) \,&&\setminus\, &&(M \,\times\, R)    \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\setminus\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M) \,\times\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\times\, R) \,&&\triangle\, &&(M \,\times\, R)    \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\triangle\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\cup\, M) \,\setminus\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\setminus\, R) \,&&\cup\, &&(M \,\setminus\, R)      \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\setminus\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\cap\, M) \,\setminus\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\setminus\, R) \,&&\cap\, &&(M \,\setminus\, R)      \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\setminus\, \text{ over } \,\cap\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M) \,\setminus\, R  ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\setminus\, R) &&\,\triangle\, &&(M \,\setminus\, R) \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\setminus\, \text{ over } \,\triangle\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\setminus\, R  ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\setminus\, R) &&\,\setminus\, &&(M \,\setminus\, R)  \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\setminus\, \text{ over } \,\setminus\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
~&~~=~~&&~~\;~~\;~~\;~ L &&\,\setminus\, &&(M \cup R) \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

'''[[Left distributivity]]''':{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
L \cup   (M \cap R)            &\;=\;\;&& (L \cup M)     \cap        (L \cup R) \qquad
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\cup\, \text{ over } \,\cap\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \cup   (M \cup R)            &\;=\;\;&& (L \cup M)     \cup        (L \cup R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\cup\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \cap   (M \cup R)            &\;=\;\;&& (L \cap M)     \cup        (L \cap R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\cap\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \cap   (M \cap R)            &\;=\;\;&& (L \cap M)     \cap        (L \cap R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\cap\, \text{ over } \,\cap\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \cap   (M \,\triangle\, R)   &\;=\;\;&& (L \cap M)   \,\triangle\, (L \cap R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\cap\, \text{ over } \,\triangle\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \times (M \cap R)            &\;=\;\;&& (L \times M)   \cap        (L \times R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\cap\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \times (M \cup R)            &\;=\;\;&& (L \times M)   \cup        (L \times R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \times (M \,\setminus R)     &\;=\;\;&& (L \times M) \,\setminus   (L \times R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\setminus\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \times (M \,\triangle R)     &\;=\;\;&& (L \times M) \,\triangle   (L \times R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\triangle\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

====Distributivity and symmetric difference {{math|∆}}====

Intersection distributes over symmetric difference:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
L \,\cap\, (M \,\triangle\, R) ~&~~=~~&&  (L \,\cap\, M) \,\triangle\, (L \,\cap\, R) ~&&~ \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
(L \,\triangle\, M) \,\cap\, R~&~~=~~&&  (L \,\cap\, R) \,\triangle\, (M \,\cap\, R) ~&&~ \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

Union does not distribute over symmetric difference because only the following is guaranteed in general:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
L \cup (M \,\triangle\, R) 
~~{\color{red}{\supseteq}}~~ \color{black}{\,} (L \cup M) \,\triangle\, (L \cup R) ~
&~=~&& (M \,\triangle\, R) \,\setminus\, L  
&~=~&& (M \,\setminus\, L) \,\triangle\, (R \,\setminus\, L) \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

Symmetric difference does not distribute over itself:
<math display=block>L \,\triangle\, (M \,\triangle\, R) 
~~{\color{red}{\neq}}~~ \color{black}{\,} (L \,\triangle\, M) \,\triangle\, (L \,\triangle\, R) 
~=~ M \,\triangle\, R</math>
and in general, for any sets <math>L \text{ and } A</math> (where <math>A</math> represents <math>M \,\triangle\, R</math>), <math>L \,\triangle\, A</math> might not be a subset, nor a superset, of <math>L</math> (and the same is true for <math>A</math>).

====Distributivity and set subtraction {{math|\}}====

'''Failure of set subtraction to left distribute''':

Set subtraction is {{em|right}} distributive over itself. However, set subtraction is {{em|not}} left distributive over itself because only the following is guaranteed in general:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
L \,\setminus\, (M \,\setminus\, R) &~~{\color{red}{\supseteq}}~~&& \color{black}{\,} (L \,\setminus\, M) \,\setminus\, (L \,\setminus\, R) ~~=~~ L \cap R \,\setminus\, M \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
where equality holds if and only if <math>L \,\setminus\, M = L \,\cap\, R,</math> which happens [[if and only if]] <math>L \cap M \cap R = \varnothing \text{ and } L \setminus M \subseteq R.</math> 

For symmetric difference, the sets <math>L \,\setminus\, (M \,\triangle\, R)</math> and <math>(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\triangle\, (L \,\setminus\, R) = L \,\cap\, (M \,\triangle\, R)</math> are always disjoint. 
So these two sets are equal if and only if they are both equal to <math>\varnothing.</math> 
Moreover, <math>L \,\setminus\, (M \,\triangle\, R) = \varnothing</math> if and only if <math>L \cap M \cap R = \varnothing \text{ and } L \subseteq M \cup R.</math> 

To investigate the left distributivity of set subtraction over unions or intersections, consider how the sets involved in (both of) De Morgan's laws are all related:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\cap\, (L \,\setminus\, R) ~~=~~ L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cup\, R) ~&~~{\color{red}{\subseteq}}~~&& \color{black}{\,} L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cap\, R) ~~=~~ (L \,\setminus\, M) \,\cup\, (L \,\setminus\, R) \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
always holds (the equalities on the left and right are De Morgan's laws) but equality is not guaranteed in general (that is, the containment <math>{\color{red}{\subseteq}}</math> might be strict). 
Equality holds if and only if <math>L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cap\, R) \;\subseteq\; L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cup\, R),</math> which happens if and only if <math>L \,\cap\, M = L \,\cap\, R.</math> 

This observation about De Morgan's laws shows that <math>\,\setminus\,</math> is {{em|not}} left distributive over <math>\,\cup\,</math> or <math>\,\cap\,</math> because only the following are guaranteed in general:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cup\, R) ~&~~{\color{red}{\subseteq}}~~&& \color{black}{\,} (L \,\setminus\, M) \,\cup\, (L \,\setminus\, R) ~~=~~ L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cap\, R) \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cap\, R) ~&~~{\color{red}{\supseteq}}~~&& \color{black}{\,} (L \,\setminus\, M) \,\cap\, (L \,\setminus\, R) ~~=~~ L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cup\, R) \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
where equality holds for one (or equivalently, for both) of the above two inclusion formulas if and only if <math>L \,\cap\, M = L \,\cap\, R.</math> 

The following statements are equivalent:

# <math>L \cap M \,=\, L \cap R</math>
# <math>L \,\setminus\, M \,=\, L \,\setminus\, R</math>
# <math>L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cap\, R) = (L \,\setminus\, M) \,\cap\, (L \,\setminus\, R);</math> that is, <math>\,\setminus\,</math> left distributes over <math>\,\cap\,</math> for these three particular sets
# <math>L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cup\, R) = (L \,\setminus\, M) \,\cup\, (L \,\setminus\, R);</math> that is, <math>\,\setminus\,</math> left distributes over <math>\,\cup\,</math> for these three particular sets
# <math>L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cap\, R) \,=\, L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cup\, R)</math>
# <math>L \cap (M \cup R) \,=\, L \cap M \cap R</math>
# <math>L \cap (M \cup R) ~\subseteq~ M \cap R</math>
# <math>L \cap R ~\subseteq~ M \;</math> and <math>\; L \cap M ~\subseteq~ R</math>
# <math>L \setminus (M \setminus R) \,=\, L \setminus (R \setminus M)</math>
# <math>L \setminus (M \setminus R) \,=\, L \setminus (R \setminus M) \,=\, L</math>

'''[[Quasi-commutative property|Quasi-commutativity]]''': 
<math display=block>(L \setminus M) \setminus R ~=~ (L \setminus R) \setminus M \qquad \text{ (Quasi-commutative)}</math>
always holds but in general, 
<math display=block>L \setminus (M \setminus R) ~~{\color{red}{\neq}}~~ L \setminus (R \setminus M).</math>
However, <math>L \setminus (M \setminus R) ~\subseteq~ L \setminus (R \setminus M)</math> if and only if <math>L \cap R ~\subseteq~ M</math> if and only if <math>L \setminus (R \setminus M) ~=~ L.</math> 

'''Set subtraction complexity''': To manage the many identities involving set subtraction, this section is divided based on where the set subtraction operation and parentheses are located on the left hand side of the identity. The great variety and (relative) complexity of formulas involving set subtraction (compared to those without it) is in part due to the fact that unlike <math>\,\cup, \,\cap,</math> and <math>\triangle,\,</math> set subtraction is neither associative nor commutative and it also is not left distributive over <math>\,\cup, \,\cap, \,\triangle,</math> or even over itself.

===Two set subtractions===

Set subtraction is {{em|not}} associative in general: 
<math display=block>(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\setminus\, R \;~~{\color{red}{\neq}}~~\; L \,\setminus\, (M \,\setminus\, R)</math>
since only the following is always guaranteed:
<math display=block>(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\setminus\, R \;~~{\color{red}{\subseteq}}~~\; L \,\setminus\, (M \,\setminus\, R).</math>

==== {{math|(L\M)\R}} ====

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
(L \setminus M) \setminus R 
&=  &&L \setminus (M \cup R) \\[0.6ex]
&= (&&L \setminus R) \setminus M \\[0.6ex]
&= (&&L \setminus M) \cap (L \setminus R) \\[0.6ex]
&= (&&L \setminus R) \setminus M \\[0.6ex]
&= (&&L \,\setminus\, R) \,\setminus\, (M \,\setminus\, R) \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

==== {{math|L\(M\R)}} ====

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
L \setminus (M \setminus R) 
&= (L \setminus M) \cup (L \cap R) \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
:* If <math>L \subseteq M \text{ then } L \setminus (M \setminus R) = L \cap R</math>
:* <math display=inline>L \setminus (M \setminus R) \subseteq (L \setminus M) \cup R</math> with equality if and only if <math>R \subseteq L.</math>

===One set subtraction===

==== {{math|(L\M) ⁎ R}} ====

'''Set subtraction on the ''left'', and parentheses on the {{em|left}}'''

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
\left(L \setminus M\right) \cup R 
&= (L \cup R) \setminus (M \setminus R) \\
&= (L \setminus (M \cup R)) \cup R ~~~~~ \text{ (the outermost union is disjoint) } \\
\end{alignat}</math>

:<math>\begin{alignat}{4}
(L \setminus M) \cap R 
&= (&&L \cap R) \setminus (M \cap R) ~~~\text{ (Distributive law of } \cap \text{ over } \setminus \text{ )} \\
&= (&&L \cap R) \setminus M \\
&=  &&L \cap (R \setminus M) \\
\end{alignat}</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=15-26}}

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\cap\, (L \,\setminus\, R) ~~=~~ L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cup\, R) ~&~~{\color{red}{\subseteq}}~~&& \color{black}{\,} L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cap\, R) ~~=~~ (L \,\setminus\, M) \,\cup\, (L \,\setminus\, R) \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math> 
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
(L \setminus M) ~\triangle~ R 
&= (L \setminus (M \cup R)) \cup (R \setminus L) \cup (L \cap M \cap  R) ~~~\text{ (the three outermost sets are pairwise disjoint) } \\
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>(L \,\setminus M) \times R = (L \times R) \,\setminus (M \times R)    ~~~~~\text{ (Distributivity)}</math>

==== {{math|L\(M ⁎ R)}} ====

'''Set subtraction on the ''left'', and parentheses on the {{em|right}}'''

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{3}
L \setminus (M \cup R) 
&= (L \setminus M) &&\,\cap\,    (&&L \setminus R) ~~~~\text{ (De Morgan's law) } \\
&= (L \setminus M) &&\,\,\setminus &&R \\
&= (L \setminus R) &&\,\,\setminus &&M \\
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
L \setminus (M \cap R) 
&= (L \setminus M) \cup (L \setminus R) ~~~~\text{ (De Morgan's law) } \\
\end{alignat}</math>
where the above two sets that are the subjects of [[De Morgan's laws]] always satisfy <math>L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cup\, R) ~~{\color{red}{\subseteq}}~~ \color{black}{\,} L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cap\, R).</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
L \setminus (M ~\triangle~ R) 
&= (L \setminus (M \cup R)) \cup (L \cap M \cap R) ~~~\text{ (the outermost union is disjoint) } \\
\end{alignat}</math>

==== {{math|(L ⁎ M)\R}} ====

'''Set subtraction on the ''right'', and parentheses on the {{em|left}}'''

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
(L \cup M) \setminus R 
&= (L \setminus R) \cup (M \setminus R) \\
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
(L \cap M) \setminus R 
&= (&&L \setminus R) &&\cap (M \setminus R) \\
&=  &&L              &&\cap (M \setminus R) \\
&=  &&M              &&\cap (L \setminus R) \\
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
(L \,\triangle\, M)   \setminus R 
&= (L \setminus R) ~&&\triangle~ (M \setminus R) \\
&= (L \cup R)      ~&&\triangle~ (M \cup R) \\
\end{alignat}</math>

==== {{math|L ⁎ (M\R)}} ====

'''Set subtraction on the ''right'', and parentheses on the {{em|right}}'''

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{3}
L \cup (M \setminus R)
&=  && &&L              &&\cup\;            &&(M \setminus (R \cup L)) &&~~~\text{ (the outermost union is disjoint) } \\
&= [&&(&&L \setminus M) &&\cup\;            &&(R \cap L)] \cup (M \setminus R)       &&~~~\text{ (the outermost union is disjoint) } \\
&=  &&(&&L \setminus (M \cup R)) \;&&\;\cup &&(R \cap L)\,\, \cup (M \setminus R)   &&~~~\text{ (the three outermost sets are pairwise disjoint) } \\
\end{alignat}</math>

:<math>\begin{alignat}{4}
L \cap (M \setminus R)
&= (&&L \cap M)      &&\setminus (L \cap R) ~~~\text{ (Distributive law of } \cap \text{ over } \setminus \text{ )}  \\
&= (&&L \cap M)      &&\setminus R  \\
&=  &&M              &&\cap (L \setminus R) \\
&= (&&L \setminus R) &&\cap (M \setminus R) \\
\end{alignat}
</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=15-26}}

<math display=block>L \times (M \,\setminus R) = (L \times M) \,\setminus (L \times R)    ~~~~~\text{ (Distributivity)}</math>

===Three operations on three sets===

==== {{math|(L • M) ⁎ (M • R)}} ====

'''Operations of the form <math>(L \bullet M) \ast (M \bullet R)</math>''':

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
(L \cup M)            &\,\cup\,&&       (&&M \cup R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& L \cup M \cup R \\[1.4ex]
(L \cup M)            &\,\cap\,&&       (&&M \cup R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& M \cup (L \cap R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \cup M)            &\,\setminus\,&&  (&&M \cup R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& L \,\setminus\, (M \cup R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \cup M)            &\,\triangle\,&&  (&&M \cup R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \,\setminus\, (M \cup R)) \,\cup\, (R \,\setminus\, (L \cup M)) \\[1.4ex]
&\,&&\,&&\,&& &&\;=\;\;&& (L \,\triangle\, R) \,\setminus\, M \\[1.4ex]
(L \cap M)            &\,\cup\,&&       (&&M \cap R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& M \cap (L \cup R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \cap M)            &\,\cap\,&&       (&&M \cap R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& L \cap M \cap R \\[1.4ex]
(L \cap M)            &\,\setminus\,&&  (&&M \cap R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \cap M) \,\setminus\, R \\[1.4ex]
(L \cap M)            &\,\triangle\,&&  (&&M \cap R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& [(L \,\cap M) \cup (M \,\cap R)] \,\setminus\, (L \,\cap M \,\cap R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus M)     &\,\cup\,&&  (&&M \,\setminus R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \,\cup M) \,\setminus (M \,\cap\, R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus M)     &\,\cap\,&&  (&&M \,\setminus R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& \varnothing \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus M)     &\,\setminus\,&&  (&&M \,\setminus R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& L \,\setminus M \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus M)     &\,\triangle\,&&  (&&M \,\setminus R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \,\setminus M) \cup (M \,\setminus R) \\[1.4ex]
&\,&&\,&&\,&& &&\;=\;\;&& (L \,\cup M) \setminus (M \,\cap R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M)   &\,\cup\,&&  (&&M \,\triangle\, R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \,\cup\, M \,\cup\, R) \,\setminus\, (L \,\cap\, M \,\cap\, R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M)   &\,\cap\,&&  (&&M \,\triangle\, R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& ((L \,\cap\, R) \,\setminus\, M) \,\cup\, (M \,\setminus\, (L \,\cup\, R)) \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M)   &\,\setminus\,&&  (&&M \,\triangle\, R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cup\, R)) \,\cup\, ((M \,\cap\, R) \,\setminus\, L) \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M)   &\,\triangle\,&&  (&&M \,\triangle\, R) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& L \,\triangle\, R \\[1.7ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

==== {{math|(L • M) ⁎ (R\M)}} ====

'''Operations of the form <math>(L \bullet M) \ast (R \,\setminus\, M)</math>''':

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
(L \cup M)            &\,\cup\,&&       (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& L \cup M \cup R \\[1.4ex]
(L \cup M)            &\,\cap\,&&       (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \cap R) \,\setminus\, M \\[1.4ex]
(L \cup M)            &\,\setminus\,&&  (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& M \cup (L \,\setminus\, R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \cup M)            &\,\triangle\,&&  (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& M \cup (L \,\triangle\, R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \cap M)            &\,\cup\,&&       (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& [L \cap (M \cup R)] \cup [R \,\setminus\, (L \cup M)] \qquad \text{ (disjoint union)} \\[1.4ex]
&\,&&\,&&\,&& &&\;=\;\;&& (L \cap M) \,\triangle\, (R \,\setminus\, M) \\[1.4ex]
(L \cap M)            &\,\cap\,&&       (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& \varnothing \\[1.4ex]
(L \cap M)            &\,\setminus\,&&   (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& L \cap M \\[1.4ex]
(L \cap M)            &\,\triangle\,&&  (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \cap M) \cup (R \,\setminus\, M) \qquad \text{ (disjoint union)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus\, M)   &\,\cup\,&&       (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& L \cup R \,\setminus\, M \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus\, M)   &\,\cap\,&&       (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \cap R) \,\setminus\, M \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus\, M)   &\,\setminus\,&&  (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& L \,\setminus\, (M \cup R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus\, M)   &\,\triangle\,&&  (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \,\triangle\, R) \,\setminus\, M \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M)   &\,\cup\,&&       (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \cup M \cup R) \,\setminus\, (L \cap M) \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M)   &\,\cap\,&&       (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& (L \cap R) \,\setminus\, M \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M)   &\,\setminus\,&&  (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& [L \,\setminus\, (M \cup R)] \cup (M \,\setminus\, L) \qquad \text{ (disjoint union)} \\[1.4ex]
&\,&&\,&&\,&& &&\;=\;\;&& (L \,\triangle\, M) \setminus (L \,\cap R) \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M)   &\,\triangle\,&&  (&&R \,\setminus\, M) && 
              &&\;=\;\;&& L \,\triangle\, (M \cup R) \\[1.7ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

==== {{math|(L\M) ⁎ (L\R)}} ====

'''Operations of the form <math>(L \,\setminus\, M) \ast (L \,\setminus\, R)</math>''':

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
(L \,\setminus M)  &\,\cup\,&&  (&&L \,\setminus R)  
            &&\;=\;&&  L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cap\, R)        \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus M)  &\,\cap\,&&  (&&L \,\setminus R)  
            &&\;=\;&&  L \,\setminus\, (M \,\cup\, R)        \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus M)  &\,\setminus\,&&  (&&L \,\setminus R)  
            &&\;=\;&&  (L \,\cap\, R) \,\setminus\, M        \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus M)  &\,\triangle\,&&  (&&L \,\setminus R)  
            &&\;=\;&&  L \,\cap\, (M \,\triangle\, R)        \\[1.4ex]
&\,&&\,&&\, &&\;=\;&& (L \cap M)   \,\triangle\, (L \cap R)  \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

===Other simplifications===

'''Other properties''':

<math display=block>L \cap M = R \;\text{ and }\; L \cap R = M \qquad \text{ if and only if } \qquad M = R \subseteq L.</math> 

* If <math>L \subseteq M</math> then <math>L \setminus R = L \cap (M \setminus R).</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=15-26}}
* <math>L \times (M \,\setminus R) = (L \times M) \,\setminus (L \times R)</math>
* If <math>L \subseteq R</math> then <math>M \setminus R \subseteq M \setminus L.</math>
* <math>L \cap M \cap R = \varnothing</math> if and only if for any <math>x \in L \cup M \cup R,</math> <math>x</math> belongs to {{em|at most two}} of the sets <math>L, M, \text{ and } R.</math>

==Symmetric difference ∆ of finitely many sets==

Given finitely many sets <math>L_1, \ldots, L_n,</math> something belongs to their [[symmetric difference]] if and only if it belongs to an odd number of these sets. Explicitly, for any <math>x,</math> <math>x \in L_1 \triangle \cdots \triangle L_n</math> if and only if the cardinality <math>\left|\left\{i : x \in L_i\right\}\right|</math> is odd. (Recall that symmetric difference is associative so parentheses are not needed for the set <math>L_1 \triangle \cdots \triangle L_n</math>).

Consequently, the symmetric difference of three sets satisfies:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
L \,\triangle\, M \,\triangle\, R 
&= (L \cap M \cap R) \cup \{x : x \text{ belongs to exactly one of the sets } L, M, R \} ~~~~~~ \text{ (the union is disjoint) } \\
&= [L \cap M \cap R] \cup [L \setminus (M \cup R)] \cup [M \setminus (L \cup R)] \cup [R \setminus (L \cup M)] ~~~~~~~~~ \text{ (all 4 sets enclosed by [ ] are pairwise disjoint) } \\
\end{alignat}</math>

==Cartesian products {{math|⨯}} of finitely many sets==

===Binary {{math|⨯}} distributes over {{math|⋃}} and {{math|⋂}} and {{math|\}} and {{math|∆}}===

The binary [[Cartesian product]] ⨯ [[#Distributivity|distributes over]] unions, intersections, set subtraction, and symmetric difference:

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
(L \,\cap\, M) \,\times\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\times\, R) \,&&\cap\, &&(M \,\times\, R)        \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\cap\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\cup\, M) \,\times\, R      ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\times\, R) \,&&\cup\, &&(M \,\times\, R)        \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\setminus\, M) \,\times\, R ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\times\, R) \,&&\setminus\, &&(M \,\times\, R)   \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\setminus\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
(L \,\triangle\, M) \,\times\, R ~&~~=~~&& (L \,\times\, R) \,&&\triangle\, &&(M \,\times\, R)   \qquad 
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\triangle\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
L \times   (M \cap R)            &\;=\;\;&& (L \times M)     \cap       (L \times R) \qquad
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\cap\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \times   (M \cup R)            &\;=\;\;&& (L \times M)    \cup       (L \times R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \times   (M \setminus R)       &\;=\;\;&& (L \times M)    \setminus  (L \times R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\setminus\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \times   (M \triangle R)       &\;=\;\;&& (L \times M)    \triangle  (L \times R) 
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\triangle\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

But in general, ⨯ does not distribute over itself:
<math display=block>L \times (M \times R) ~\color{Red}{\neq}\color{Black}{}~ (L \times M) \times (L \times R)</math>
<math display=block>(L \times M) \times R ~\color{Red}{\neq}\color{Black}{}~ (L \times R) \times (M \times R).</math>

===Binary {{math|⋂}} of finite {{math|⨯}}===

<math display=block>(L \times R) \cap \left(L_2 \times R_2\right) ~=~ \left(L \cap L_2\right) \times \left(R \cap R_2\right)</math>
<math display=block>(L \times M \times R) \cap \left(L_2 \times M_2 \times R_2\right) ~=~ \left(L \cap L_2\right) \times \left(M \cap M_2\right) \times \left(R \cap R_2\right)</math>

===Binary {{math|⋃}} of finite {{math|⨯}}===

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
\left(L \times R\right) ~\cup~ \left(L_2 \times R_2\right) 
~&=~ \left[\left(L \setminus L_2\right) \times R\right] ~\cup~ \left[\left(L_2 \setminus L\right) \times R_2\right] ~\cup~ \left[\left(L \cap L_2\right) \times \left(R \cup R_2\right)\right] \\[0.5ex]
~&=~ \left[L \times \left(R \setminus R_2\right)\right] ~\cup~ \left[L_2 \times \left(R_2 \setminus R\right)\right] ~\cup~ \left[\left(L \cup L_2\right) \times \left(R \cap R_2\right)\right] \\
\end{alignat}</math>

===Difference {{math|\}} of finite {{math|⨯}}===

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
\left(L \times R\right) ~\setminus~ \left(L_2 \times R_2\right) 
~&=~ \left[\left(L \,\setminus\, L_2\right) \times R\right] ~\cup~ \left[L \times \left(R \,\setminus\, R_2\right)\right] \\
\end{alignat}</math>
and 
<math display=block>(L \times M \times R) ~\setminus~ \left(L_2 \times M_2 \times R_2\right) 
~=~ \left[\left(L \,\setminus\, L_2\right) \times M \times R\right] ~\cup~ \left[L \times \left(M \,\setminus\, M_2\right) \times R\right] ~\cup~ \left[L \times M \times \left(R \,\setminus\, R_2\right)\right]</math>

===Finite {{math|⨯}} of differences {{math|\}}===

<math display=block>\left(L \,\setminus\, L_2\right) \times \left(R \,\setminus\, R_2\right) ~=~ \left(L \times R\right) \,\setminus\, \left[\left(L_2 \times R\right) \cup \left(L \times R_2\right)\right]</math>

<math display=block>\left(L \,\setminus\, L_2\right) \times \left(M \,\setminus\, M_2\right) \times \left(R \,\setminus\, R_2\right) ~=~ \left(L \times M \times R\right) \,\setminus\, \left[\left(L_2 \times M \times R\right) \cup \left(L \times M_2 \times R\right) \cup \left(L \times M \times R_2\right)\right]</math>

===Symmetric difference {{math|∆}} and finite {{math|⨯}}===

<math display=block>L \times \left(R \,\triangle\, R_2\right) ~=~ \left[L \times \left(R \,\setminus\, R_2\right)\right] \,\cup\, \left[L \times \left(R_2 \,\setminus\, R\right)\right]</math>
<math display=block>\left(L \,\triangle\, L_2\right) \times R ~=~ \left[\left(L \,\setminus\, L_2\right) \times R\right] \,\cup\, \left[\left(L_2 \,\setminus\, L\right) \times R\right]</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
\left(L \,\triangle\, L_2\right) \times \left(R \,\triangle\, R_2\right) 
~&=~ && && \,\left[\left(L \cup L_2\right) \times \left(R \cup R_2\right)\right] \;\setminus\; \left[\left(\left(L \cap L_2\right) \times R\right) \;\cup\; \left(L \times \left(R \cap R_2\right)\right)\right] \\[0.7ex]
&=~ & &&& \,\left[\left(L \,\setminus\, L_2\right) \times \left(R_2 \,\setminus\, R\right)\right] \,\cup\, \left[\left(L_2 \,\setminus\, L\right) \times \left(R_2 \,\setminus\, R\right)\right] \,\cup\, \left[\left(L \,\setminus\, L_2\right) \times \left(R \,\setminus\, R_2\right)\right] \,\cup\, \left[\left(L_2 \,\setminus\, L\right) \cup \left(R \,\setminus\, R_2\right)\right] \\
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
\left(L \,\triangle\, L_2\right) \times \left(M \,\triangle\, M_2\right) \times \left(R \,\triangle\, R_2\right) 
~&=~ \left[\left(L \cup L_2\right) \times \left(M \cup M_2\right) \times \left(R \cup R_2\right)\right] \;\setminus\; \left[\left(\left(L \cap L_2\right) \times M \times R\right) \;\cup\; \left(L \times \left(M \cap M_2\right) \times R\right) \;\cup\; \left(L \times M \times \left(R \cap R_2\right)\right)\right] \\
\end{alignat}</math>

In general, <math>\left(L \,\triangle\, L_2\right) \times \left(R \,\triangle\, R_2\right)</math> need not be a subset nor a superset of <math>\left(L \times R\right) \,\triangle\, \left(L_2 \times R_2\right).</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
\left(L \times R\right) \,\triangle\, \left(L_2 \times R_2\right)
~&=~ && \left(L \times R\right) \cup \left(L_2 \times R_2\right) \;\setminus\; \left[\left(L \cap L_2\right) \times \left(R \cap R_2\right)\right] \\[0.7ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
\left(L \times M \times R\right) \,\triangle\, \left(L_2 \times M_2 \times R_2\right)
~&=~ && \left(L \times M \times R\right) \cup \left(L_2 \times M_2 \times R_2\right) \;\setminus\; \left[\left(L \cap L_2\right) \times \left(M \cap M_2\right) \times \left(R \cap R_2\right)\right] \\[0.7ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

==Arbitrary families of sets==

Let <math>\left(L_i\right)_{i \in I},</math> <math>\left(R_j\right)_{j \in J},</math> and <math>\left(S_{i,j}\right)_{(i, j) \in I \times J}</math> be indexed [[Family of sets|families of sets]]. Whenever the assumption is needed, then all [[indexing set]]s, such as <math>I</math> and <math>J,</math> are assumed to be non-empty. 

===Definitions===

A {{em|[[family of sets]]}} or (more briefly) a {{em|family}} refers to a set whose elements are sets. 

An {{em|[[indexed family]] of sets}} is a function from some set, called its {{em|[[indexing set]]}}, into some family of sets. 
An indexed family of sets will be denoted by <math>\left(L_i\right)_{i \in I},</math> where this notation assigns the symbol <math>I</math> for the indexing set and for every index <math>i \in I,</math> assigns the symbol <math>L_i</math> to the value of the function at <math>i.</math> 
The function itself may then be denoted by the symbol <math>L_\bull,</math> which is obtained from the notation <math>\left(L_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> by replacing the index <math>i</math> with a bullet symbol <math>\bullet\,;</math> explicitly, <math>L_\bull</math> is the function:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
L_\bull :\;&& I &&\;\to    \;& \left\{L_i : i \in I\right\} \\[0.3ex]
           && i &&\;\mapsto\;& L_i \\
\end{alignat}</math>
which may be summarized by writing <math>L_\bull = \left(L_i\right)_{i \in I}.</math> 

Any given indexed family of sets <math>L_\bull = \left(L_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> (which is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]]) can be canonically associated with its image/range <math>\operatorname{Im} L_\bull ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \left\{L_i : i \in I\right\}</math> (which is a family of sets). 
Conversely, any given family of sets <math>\mathcal{B}</math> may be associated with the <math>\mathcal{B}</math>-indexed family of sets <math>(B)_{B \in \mathcal{B}},</math> which is technically the [[identity map]] <math>\mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{B}.</math> 
However, this is {{em|not}} a bijective correspondence because an indexed family of sets <math>L_\bull = \left(L_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> is {{em|not}} required to be injective (that is, there may exist distinct indices <math>i \neq j</math> such as <math>L_i = L_j</math>), which in particular means that it is possible for distinct indexed families of sets (which are functions) to be associated with the same family of sets (by having the same image/range). 

'''Arbitrary unions defined'''{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i ~~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{x ~:~ \text{ there exists } i \in I \text{ such that } x \in L_i\}</math>|{{EquationRef|Def. 1}}}}

If <math>I = \varnothing</math> then <math>\bigcup_{i \in \varnothing} L_i = \{x ~:~ \text{ there exists } i \in \varnothing \text{ such that } x \in L_i\} = \varnothing,</math> which is somethings called the {{em|nullary union convention}} (despite being called a convention, this equality follows from the definition). 

If <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a family of sets then <math>\cup \mathcal{B}</math> denotes the set: 
<math display=block>\bigcup \mathcal{B} ~~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \bigcup_{B \in \mathcal{B}} B ~~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{x ~:~ \text{ there exists } B \in \mathcal{B} \text{ such that } x \in B\}.</math>

'''Arbitrary intersections defined'''

If <math>I \neq \varnothing</math> then{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i ~~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{x ~:~ x \in L_i \text{ for every } i \in I\} ~=~ \{x ~:~  \text{ for all } i, \text{ if } i \in I \text{ then } x \in L_i\}.</math>|{{EquationRef|Def. 2}}}}

If <math>\mathcal{B} \neq \varnothing</math> is a {{em|non-empty}} family of sets then <math>\cap \mathcal{B}</math> denotes the set: 
<math display=block>\bigcap \mathcal{B} ~~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \bigcap_{B \in B} B ~~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{x ~:~ x \in B \text{ for every } B \in \mathcal{B}\} ~=~ \{x ~:~  \text{ for all } B, \text{ if } B \in \mathcal{B} \text{ then } x \in B\}.</math>

'''Nullary intersections'''

If <math>I = \varnothing</math> then
<math display=block>\bigcap_{i \in \varnothing} L_i = \{x ~:~  \text{ for all } i, \text{ if } i \in \varnothing \text{ then } x \in L_i\}</math>
where every possible thing <math>x</math> in the universe [[Vacuous truth|vacuously]] satisfied the condition: "if <math>i \in \varnothing</math> then <math>x \in L_i</math>". Consequently, <math>{\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{i \in \varnothing}} L_i = \{x : \text{ true }\}</math> consists of {{em|everything}} in the universe. 

So if <math>I = \varnothing</math> and:
#if you are working in a [[Model theory|model]] in which there exists some [[Universe set|universe '''{{em|set}}''']] <math>X</math> then <math>{\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{i \in \varnothing}} L_i = \{x ~:~ x \in L_i \text{ for every } i \in \varnothing\} ~=~ X.</math> 
#otherwise, if you are working in a [[Model theory|model]] in which "the class of all things <math>x</math>" is not a set (by far the most common situation) then <math>{\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{i \in \varnothing}} L_i</math> is {{em|undefined}} because <math>{\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{i \in \varnothing}} L_i</math> consists of {{em|everything}}, which makes <math>{\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{i \in \varnothing}} L_i</math> a [[proper class]] and {{em|not}} a set. 

:'''Assumption''': Henceforth, whenever a formula requires some indexing set to be non-empty in order for an arbitrary intersection to be well-defined, then this will automatically be assumed without mention. 

A consequence of this is the following assumption/definition:

:A '''{{em|finite intersection}} of sets''' or an '''{{em|intersection of finitely many sets}}''' refers to the intersection of a finite collection of {{em|one or more}} sets. 

Some authors adopt the so called '''{{em|[[nullary intersection]] convention}}''', which is the convention that an empty intersection of sets is equal to some canonical set. In particular, if all sets are subsets of some set <math>X</math> then some author may declare that the empty intersection of these sets be equal to <math>X.</math> However, the nullary intersection convention is not as commonly accepted as the nullary union convention and this article will not adopt it (this is due to the fact that unlike the empty union, the value of the empty intersection depends on <math>X</math> so if there are multiple sets under consideration, which is commonly the case, then the value of the empty intersection risks becoming ambiguous).

'''Multiple index sets'''
<math display=block>\bigcup_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in J}} S_{i,j} ~~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \bigcup_{(i, j) \in I \times J} S_{i,j}</math>
<math display=block>\bigcap_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in J}} S_{i,j} ~~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \bigcap_{(i, j) \in I \times J} S_{i,j}</math>

===Distributing unions and intersections===

====Binary ⋂ of arbitrary ⋃'s{{anchor|Distributing a binary intersection of arbitrary unions}}====

{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cap R ~=~ \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cap R\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 3a}}}}
and{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=15-26}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cap \left(\bigcup_{j \in J} R_j\right) ~=~ \bigcup_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in J}} \left(L_i \cap R_j\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 3b}}}}

* If all <math>\left(L_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> are [[pairwise disjoint]] and all <math>\left(R_j\right)_{j \in J}</math> are also pairwise disjoint, then so are all <math>\left(L_i \cap R_j\right)_{(i, j) \in I \times J}</math> (that is, if <math>(i, j) \neq \left(i_2, j_2\right)</math> then <math>\left(L_i \cap R_j\right) \cap \left(L_{i_2} \cap R_{j_2}\right) = \varnothing</math>).

{{anchor|Ranging over pairs of indices}}
* '''Importantly''', if <math>I = J</math> then in general, <math display=block>~\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cap \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} R_i\right) ~~\color{Red}{\neq}\color{Black}{}~~ \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cap R_i\right)~</math> (an [[#CounterExampleToEqualityInterOfUnionsWhenIequalsJ|example of this]] is given below).  The single union on the right hand side {{em|must}} be over all pairs <math>(i, j) \in I \times I:</math> <math display=block>~\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cap \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} R_i\right) ~~=~~ \bigcup_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in I}} \left(L_i \cap R_j\right).~</math> The same is usually true for other similar non-trivial set equalities and relations that depend on two (potentially unrelated) indexing sets <math>I</math> and <math>J</math> (such as {{EquationNote|Eq. 4b}} or {{EquationNote|Eq. 7g}}{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=15-26}}). Two exceptions are {{EquationNote|Eq. 2c}} (unions of unions) and {{EquationNote|Eq. 2d}} (intersections of intersections), but both of these are among the most trivial of set equalities (although even for these equalities there is still something that must be proven<ref group=note name="DeducingIntersectionOfIntersections"/>).
* '''{{visible anchor|CounterExampleToEqualityInterOfUnionsWhenIequalsJ|CounterExampleToEqualityUnionOfIntersWhenIequalsJ|text=Example where equality fails}}''': Let <math>X \neq \varnothing</math> and let <math>I = \{1, 2\}.</math> Let <math>L_1 \colon= R_2 \colon= X</math> and let <math>L_2 \colon= R_1 \colon= \varnothing.</math> Then <math display=block>X = X \cap X = \left(L_1 \cup L_2\right) \cap \left(R_2 \cup R_2\right) = \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cap \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} R_i\right) ~\neq~ \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cap R_i\right) = \left(L_1 \cap R_1\right) \cup \left(L_2 \cap R_2\right) = \varnothing \cup \varnothing = \varnothing.</math> Furthermore, <math display=block>\varnothing = \varnothing \cup \varnothing = \left(L_1 \cap L_2\right) \cup \left(R_2 \cap R_2\right) = \left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cup \left(\bigcap_{i \in I} R_i\right) ~\neq~ \bigcap_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cup R_i\right) = \left(L_1 \cup R_1\right) \cap \left(L_2 \cup R_2\right) = X \cap X = X.</math>

====Binary ⋃ of arbitrary ⋂'s{{anchor|Distributing a binary union of arbitrary intersections}}====

{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cup R ~=~ \bigcap_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cup R\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 4a}}}}
and{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=15-26}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cup \left(\bigcap_{j \in J} R_j\right) ~=~ \bigcap_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in J}} \left(L_i \cup R_j\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 4b}}}}

* '''Importantly''', if <math>I = J</math> then in general, <math display=block>~\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cup \left(\bigcap_{i \in I} R_i\right) ~~\color{Red}{\neq}\color{Black}{}~~ \bigcap_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cup R_i\right)~</math> (an [[#CounterExampleToEqualityUnionOfIntersWhenIequalsJ|example of this]] is given above).  The single intersection on the right hand side {{em|must}} be over all pairs <math>(i, j) \in I \times I:</math> <math display=block>~\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cup \left(\bigcap_{i \in I} R_i\right) ~~=~~ \bigcap_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in I}} \left(L_i \cup R_j\right).~</math>

====Arbitrary ⋂'s and arbitrary ⋃'s{{anchor|Arbitrary intersections and arbitrary unions|Distributing arbitrary intersections and arbitrary unions}}====

=====Incorrectly distributing by swapping ⋂ and ⋃{{anchor|Incorrectly distributing arbitrary intersections and arbitrary unions}}=====
'''Naively swapping <math>\;{\textstyle\bigcup\limits_{i \in I}}\;</math> and <math>\;{\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{j \in J}}\;</math> may produce a different set'''{{anchor|Arbitrary unions/intersections and switching symbols}}

The following inclusion always holds:
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\bigcup_{i \in I} \left(\bigcap_{j \in J} S_{i,j}\right) ~~\color{Red}{\subseteq}\color{Black}{}~~ \bigcap_{j \in J} \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} S_{i,j}\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|In. 1|2=Inclusion 1 ∪∩ is a subset of ∩∪}}|LnSty=1px dashed black}}

In general, equality need not hold and moreover, the right hand side depends on how for each fixed <math>i \in I,</math> the sets <math>\left(S_{i,j}\right)_{j \in J}</math> are labelled; and analogously, the left hand side depends on how for each fixed <math>j \in J,</math> the sets <math>\left(S_{i,j}\right)_{i \in I}</math> are labelled. An example demonstrating this is now given.

<ul>
<li>'''Example of dependence on labeling and failure of equality''': To see why equality need not hold when <math>\cup</math> and <math>\cap</math> are swapped, let <math>I \colon= J \colon= \{1, 2\},</math> and let <math>S_{11} = \{1, 2\},~S_{12} = \{1, 3\},~S_{21} = \{3, 4\},</math> and <math>S_{22} = \{2, 4\}.</math> Then <math display=block>\{1, 4\} = \{1\} \cup \{4\} = \left(S_{11} \cap S_{12}\right) \cup \left(S_{21} \cap S_{22}\right) = \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(\bigcap_{j \in J} S_{i,j}\right) ~\neq~ \bigcap_{j \in J} \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} S_{i,j}\right) = \left(S_{11} \cup S_{21}\right) \cap \left(S_{12} \cup S_{22}\right) = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}.</math> 
If <math>S_{11}</math> and <math>S_{21}</math> are swapped while <math>S_{12}</math> and <math>S_{22}</math> are unchanged, which gives rise to the sets <math>\hat{S}_{11} \colon= \{3, 4\},~\hat{S}_{12} \colon= \{1, 3\},~\hat{S}_{21} \colon= \{1, 2\},</math> and <math>\hat{S}_{22} \colon= \{2, 4\},</math> then 
<math display=block>\{2, 3\} = \{3\} \cup \{2\} = \left(\hat{S}_{11} \cap \hat{S}_{12}\right) \cup \left(\hat{S}_{21} \cap \hat{S}_{22}\right) = \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(\bigcap_{j \in J} \hat{S}_{i,j}\right) ~\neq~ \bigcap_{j \in J} \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} \hat{S}_{i,j}\right) = \left(\hat{S}_{11} \cup \hat{S}_{21}\right) \cap \left(\hat{S}_{12} \cup \hat{S}_{22}\right) = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}.</math> 
In particular, the left hand side is no longer <math>\{1, 4\},</math> which shows that the left hand side <math>{\textstyle\bigcup\limits_{i \in I}} \; {\textstyle\bigcap\limits_{j \in J}} S_{i,j}</math> depends on how the sets are labelled. 
If instead <math>S_{11}</math> and <math>S_{12}</math> are swapped while <math>S_{21}</math> and <math>S_{22}</math> are unchanged, which gives rise to the sets <math>\overline{S}_{11} \colon= \{1, 3\},~ \overline{S}_{12} \colon= \{1, 2\},~ \overline{S}_{21} \colon= \{3, 4\},</math> and <math>\overline{S}_{22} \colon= \{2, 4\},</math> then both the left hand side and right hand side are equal to <math>\{1, 4\},</math> which shows that the right hand side also depends on how the sets are labeled.</li>
</ul>

Equality in {{EquationNote|In. 1|Inclusion 1 ∪∩ is a subset of ∩∪}} can hold under certain circumstances, such as in {{EquationNote|Eq. 7e|7e}}, which is the special case where <math>\left(S_{i,j}\right)_{(i,j) \in I \times J}</math> is <math>\left(L_i \setminus R_j\right)_{(i,j) \in I \times J}</math> (that is, <math>S_{i,j} \colon= L_i \setminus R_j</math> with the same indexing sets <math>I</math> and <math>J</math>), or such as in {{EquationNote|Eq. 7f|7f}}, which is the special case where <math>\left(S_{i,j}\right)_{(i,j) \in I \times J}</math> is <math>\left(L_i \setminus R_j\right)_{(j, i) \in J \times I}</math> (that is, <math>\hat{S}_{j,i} \colon= L_i \setminus R_j</math> with the indexing sets <math>I</math> and <math>J</math> swapped).
For a correct formula that extends the distributive laws, an approach other than just switching <math>\cup</math> and <math>\cap</math> is needed.

=====Correct distributive laws{{anchor|Correctly distributing arbitrary intersections and arbitrary unions|Correct distribution laws}}=====

Suppose that for each <math>i \in I,</math> <math>J_i</math> is a non-empty index set and for each <math>j \in J_i,</math> let <math>T_{i,j}</math> be any set (for example, to apply this law to <math>\left(S_{i,j}\right)_{(i, j) \in I \times J},</math> use <math>J_i \colon= J</math> for all <math>i \in I</math> and use <math>T_{i,j} \colon= S_{i,j}</math> for all <math>i \in I</math> and all <math>j \in J_i = J</math>). Let
<math display=block>{\textstyle \prod} J_{\bull} ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \prod_{i \in I} J_i</math> 
denote the [[Cartesian product]], which can be interpreted as the set of all functions <math>f ~:~ I ~\to~ {\textstyle\bigcup\limits_{i \in I}} J_i</math> such that <math>f(i) \in J_i</math> for every <math>i \in I.</math> Such a function may also be denoted using the [[tuple]] notation <math>\left(f_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> where <math>f_i ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ f(i)</math> for every <math>i \in I</math> and conversely, a tuple <math>\left(f_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> is just notation for the function with domain <math>I</math> whose value at <math>i \in I</math> is <math>f_i;</math> both notations can be used to denote the elements of <math>{\textstyle \prod} J_{\bull}.</math> 
Then 
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\bigcap_{i \in I} \left[\;\bigcup_{j \in J_i} T_{i,j}\right] = \bigcup_{f \in \prod J_{\bull}} \left[\;\bigcap_{i \in I} T_{i,f(i)}\right]</math>|{{EquationRef|5|2=Eq. 5 ∩∪ to ∪∩}}|LnSty=1px dashed black}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\bigcup_{i \in I} \left[\;\bigcap_{j \in J_i} T_{i,j}\right] = \bigcap_{f \in \prod J_{\bull}} \left[\;\bigcup_{i \in I} T_{i,f(i)}\right]</math>|{{EquationRef|6|2=Eq. 6 ∪∩ to ∩∪}}|LnSty=1px dashed black}}

where <math>{\textstyle \prod} J_{\bull} ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ {\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in I}} J_i.</math> 

=====Applying the distributive laws{{anchor|Application of the distributive laws}}=====

'''{{em|Example application}}''': In the particular case where all <math>J_i</math> are equal (that is, <math>J_i = J_{i_2}</math> for all <math>i, i_2 \in I,</math> which is the case with the family <math>\left(S_{i,j}\right)_{(i, j) \in I \times J},</math> for example), then letting <math>J</math> denote this common set, the Cartesian product will be <math>{\textstyle \prod} J_{\bull} ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ {\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in I}} J_i = {\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in I}} J = J^I,</math> which is the [[Function space|set of all functions]] of the form <math>f ~:~ I ~\to~ J.</math> The above set equalities {{EquationNote|5|2=Eq. 5 ∩∪ to ∪∩}} and {{EquationNote|6|2=Eq. 6 ∪∩ to ∩∪}}, respectively become:{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}
<math display=block>\bigcap_{i \in I} \; \bigcup_{j \in J} S_{i,j} = \bigcup_{f \in J^I} \; \bigcap_{i \in I} S_{i,f(i)}</math>
<math display=block>\bigcup_{i \in I} \; \bigcap_{j \in J} S_{i,j} = \bigcap_{f \in J^I} \; \bigcup_{i \in I} S_{i,f(i)}</math>

which when combined with {{EquationNote|In. 1|2=Inclusion 1 ∪∩ is a subset of ∩∪}} implies:
