<math display=block>\bigcup_{i \in I} \; \bigcap_{j \in J} S_{i,j}
~=~ \bigcap_{f \in J^I} \; \bigcup_{i \in I} S_{i,f(i)}
~~\color{Red}{\subseteq}\color{Black}{}~~  \bigcup_{g \in I^J} \; \bigcap_{j \in J} S_{g(j),j}
~=~ \bigcap_{j \in J} \; \bigcup_{i \in I} S_{i,j}</math>
where 
* on the left hand side, the indices <math>f \text{ and } i</math> range over <math>f \in J^I \text{ and } i \in I</math> (so the subscripts of <math>S_{i,f(i)}</math> range over <math>i \in I \text{ and } f(i) \in f(I) \subseteq J</math>) 
* on the right hand side, the indices <math>g \text{ and } j</math> range over <math>g \in I^J \text{ and } j \in J</math> (so the subscripts of <math>S_{g(j),j}</math> range over <math>j \in J \text{ and } g(j) \in g(J) \subseteq I</math>). 


'''{{em|Example application}}''': To apply the general formula to the case of <math>\left(C_k\right)_{k \in K}</math> and <math>\left(D_{l}\right)_{l \in L},</math> use <math>I \colon= \{1, 2\},</math> <math>J_1 \colon= K,</math> <math>J_2 \colon= L,</math> and let <math>T_{1,k} \colon= C_k</math> for all <math>k \in J_1</math> and let <math>T_{2,l} \colon= D_l</math> for all <math>l \in J_2.</math> 
Every map <math>f \in {\textstyle \prod} J_{\bull} ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ {\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in I}} J_i = J_1 \times J_2 = K \times L</math> can be [[Bijection|bijectively]] identified with the pair <math>\left(f(1), f(2)\right) \in K \times L</math> (the inverse sends <math>(k,l) \in K \times L</math> to the map <math>f_{(k,l)} \in {\textstyle \prod} J_{\bull}</math> defined by <math>1 \mapsto k</math> and <math>2 \mapsto l;</math> this is technically just a change of notation). Recall that {{EquationNote|5|2=Eq. 5 ∩∪ to ∪∩}} was  
<math display=block>~\bigcap_{i \in I} \; \bigcup_{j \in J_i} T_{i,j} = \bigcup_{f \in {\textstyle \prod} J_{\bull}} \; \bigcap_{i \in I} T_{i,f(i)}.~</math>  
Expanding and simplifying the left hand side gives
<math display=block>\bigcap_{i \in I} \; \bigcup_{j \in J_i} T_{i,j}
= \left(\bigcup_{j \in J_1} T_{1,j}\right) \cap \left(\;\bigcup_{j \in J_2} T_{2,j}\right) 
= \left(\bigcup_{k \in K} T_{1,k}\right) \cap \left(\;\bigcup_{l \in L} T_{2,l}\right) 
= \left(\bigcup_{k \in K} C_k\right) \cap \left(\;\bigcup_{l \in L} D_l\right)
</math>
and doing the same to the right hand side gives:
<math display=block>\bigcup_{f \in \prod J_{\bull}} \; \bigcap_{i \in I} T_{i,f(i)}
= \bigcup_{f \in \prod J_{\bull}} \left(T_{1,f(1)} \cap T_{2,f(2)}\right) 
= \bigcup_{f \in \prod J_{\bull}} \left(C_{f(1)} \cap D_{f(2)}\right) 
= \bigcup_{(k,l) \in K \times L} \left(C_k \cap D_l\right) 
= \bigcup_{\stackrel{k \in K,}{l \in L}} \left(C_k \cap D_l\right).
</math>

Thus the general identity {{EquationNote|5|2=Eq. 5 ∩∪ to ∪∩}} reduces down to the previously given set equality {{EquationNote|Eq. 3b}}: 
<math display=block>\left(\bigcup_{k \in K} C_k\right) \cap \;\bigcup_{l \in L} D_l = \bigcup_{\stackrel{k \in K,}{l \in L}} \left(C_k \cap  D_l\right).</math>

===Distributing subtraction over ⋃ and ⋂{{anchor|Distributing subtraction over unions and intersections}}===

{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \;\setminus\; R ~=~ \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(L_i \;\setminus\; R\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 7a}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \;\setminus\; R ~=~ \bigcap_{i \in I} \left(L_i \;\setminus\; R\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 7b}}}}
The next identities are known as [[De Morgan's laws]].{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=15-26}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>L \;\setminus\; \bigcup_{j \in J} R_j ~=~ \bigcap_{j \in J} \left(L \;\setminus\; R_j\right) ~~\;~~ \text{ De Morgan's law }</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 7c}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>L \;\setminus\; \bigcap_{j \in J} R_j ~=~ \bigcup_{j \in J} \left(L \;\setminus\; R_j\right) ~~\;~~ \text{ De Morgan's law }</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 7d}}}}

The following four set equalities can be deduced from the equalities {{EquationNote|Eq. 7a|7a}} - {{EquationNote|Eq. 7d|7d}} above. 
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \;\setminus\; \bigcup_{j \in J} R_j   ~=~   \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(\bigcap_{j \in J} \left(L_i \;\setminus\; R_j\right)\right)   ~=~    \bigcap_{j \in J} \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} \left(L_i \;\setminus\; R_j\right)\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 7e}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \;\setminus\; \bigcap_{j \in J} R_j   ~=~    \bigcup_{j \in J} \left(\bigcap_{i \in I} \left(L_i \;\setminus\; R_j\right)\right)   ~=~   \bigcap_{i \in I} \left(\bigcup_{j \in J} \left(L_i \;\setminus\; R_j\right)\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 7f}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \;\setminus\; \bigcap_{j \in J} R_j   ~=~   \bigcup_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in J}} \left(L_i \;\setminus\; R_j\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 7g}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \;\setminus\; \bigcup_{j \in J} R_j   ~=~   \bigcap_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in J}} \left(L_i \;\setminus\; R_j\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 7h}}}}

In general, naively swapping <math>\;\cup\;</math> and <math>\;\cap\;</math> may produce a different set (see [[#Arbitrary unions/intersections and switching symbols|this note]] for more details). 
The equalities 
<math display=block>\bigcup_{i \in I} \; \bigcap_{j \in J} \left(L_i \setminus R_j\right) ~=~ \bigcap_{j \in J} \; \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(L_i \setminus R_j\right)
\quad \text{ and } \quad  
\bigcup_{j \in J} \; \bigcap_{i \in I} \left(L_i \setminus R_j\right) ~=~ \bigcap_{i \in I} \; \bigcup_{j \in J} \left(L_i \setminus R_j\right)</math> 
found in {{EquationNote|Eq. 7e}} and {{EquationNote|Eq. 7f}} are thus unusual in that they state exactly that swapping <math>\;\cup\;</math> and <math>\;\cap\;</math> will {{em|not}} change the resulting set.

===Commutativity and associativity of ⋃ and ⋂{{anchor|Commutativity and associativity of unions and intersections}}===

'''Commutativity''':{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}

<math display=block>\bigcup_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in J}} S_{i,j} 
~~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \bigcup_{(i, j) \in I \times J} S_{i,j} 
~=~ \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(\bigcup_{j \in J} S_{i,j}\right) 
~=~ \bigcup_{j \in J} \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} S_{i,j}\right)</math>

<math display=block>\bigcap_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in J}} S_{i,j} 
~~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \bigcap_{(i, j) \in I \times J} S_{i,j} 
~=~ \bigcap_{i \in I} \left(\bigcap_{j \in J} S_{i,j}\right) 
~=~ \bigcap_{j \in J} \left(\bigcap_{i \in I} S_{i,j}\right)</math>

'''Unions of unions and intersections of intersections''':{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}

<math display=block>\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cup R ~=~ \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cup R\right)</math>
<math display=block>\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cap R ~=~ \bigcap_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cap R\right)</math>
and{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cup \left(\bigcup_{j \in J} R_j\right) ~=~ \bigcup_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in J}} \left(L_i \cup R_j\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 2a}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cap \left(\bigcap_{j \in J} R_j\right) ~=~ \bigcap_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in J}} \left(L_i \cap R_j\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 2b}}}}

and if <math>I = J</math> then also:<ref group=note name="DeducingIntersectionOfIntersections">To deduce {{EquationNote|Eq. 2c}} from {{EquationNote|Eq. 2a}}, it must still be shown that <math>{\textstyle\bigcup\limits_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \in I}}} \left(L_i \cup R_j\right) ~=~ {\textstyle\bigcup\limits_{i \in I}} \left(L_i \cup R_i\right)</math> so {{EquationNote|Eq. 2c}} is not a completely immediate consequence of {{EquationNote|Eq. 2a}}. (Compare this to the commentary about {{EquationNote|Eq. 3b}}).</ref>{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cup \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} R_i\right) ~=~ \bigcup_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cup R_i\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 2c}}}}
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cap \left(\bigcap_{i \in I} R_i\right) ~=~ \bigcap_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cap R_i\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 2d}}}}

===Cartesian products {{math|Π}} of arbitrarily many sets===

====Intersections {{math|⋂}} of {{math|Π}}====

If <math>\left(S_{i,j}\right)_{(i,j) \in I \times J}</math> is a family of sets then 
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\bigcap_{j \in J} \; \prod_{i \in I} S_{i,j} ~~=~~ \prod_{i \in I} \; \bigcap_{j \in J} S_{i,j}</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 8}}}}
* Moreover, a tuple <math>\left(x_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> belongs to the set in {{EquationNote|Eq. 8|Eq. 8}} above if and only if <math>x_i \in S_{i,j}</math> for all <math>i \in I</math> and all <math>j \in J.</math>

In particular, if <math>\left(L_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> and <math>\left(R_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> are two families indexed by the same set then 
<math display=block>\left(\prod_{i \in I} L_i\right) \cap \prod_{i \in I} R_i ~=~ \prod_{i \in I} \left(L_i \cap R_i\right)</math>
So for instance, 
<math display=block>(L \times R) \cap \left(L_2 \times R_2\right) ~=~ \left(L \cap L_2\right) \times \left(R \cap R_2\right)</math>
<math display=block>(L \times R) \cap \left(L_2 \times R_2\right) \cap \left(L_3 \times R_3\right) ~=~ \left(L \cap L_2 \cap L_3\right) \times \left(R \cap R_2 \cap R_3\right)</math> and 
<math display=block>(L \times M \times R) \cap \left(L_2 \times M_2 \times R_2\right) ~=~ \left(L \cap L_2\right) \times \left(M \cap M_2\right) \times \left(R \cap R_2\right)</math>

'''Intersections of products indexed by different sets'''

Let <math>\left(L_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> and <math>\left(R_j\right)_{j \in J}</math> be two families indexed by different sets. 

Technically, <math>I \neq J</math> implies <math>\left({\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in I}} L_i\right) \cap {\textstyle\prod\limits_{j \in J}} R_j = \varnothing.</math> 
However, sometimes these products are somehow identified as the same set through some [[bijection]] or one of these products is identified as a subset of the other via some [[injective map]], in which case (by [[abuse of notation]]) this intersection may be equal to some other (possibly non-empty) set. 
* For example, if <math>I := \{1, 2\}</math> and <math>J := \{1, 2, 3\}</math> with all sets equal to <math>\R</math> then <math>{\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in I}} L_i = {\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in \{1, 2\}}} \R = \R^2</math> and <math>{\textstyle\prod\limits_{j \in J}} R_j = {\textstyle\prod\limits_{j \in \{1, 2, 3\}}} \R = \R^3</math> where <math>\R^2 \cap \R^3 = \varnothing</math> {{em|unless}}, for example, <math>{\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in \{1, 2\}}} \R = \R^2</math> is identified as a subset of <math>{\textstyle\prod\limits_{j \in \{1, 2, 3\}}} \R = \R^3</math> through some [[Injective map|injection]], such as maybe <math>(x, y) \mapsto (x, y, 0)</math> for instance; however, in this particular case the product <math>{\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in I = \{1, 2\}}} L_i</math> actually represents the <math>J</math>-indexed product <math>{\textstyle\prod\limits_{j \in J = \{1, 2, 3\}}} L_i</math> where <math>L_3 := \{0\}.</math>
* For another example, take <math>I := \{1, 2\}</math> and <math>J := \{1, 2, 3\}</math> with <math>L_1 := \R^2</math> and <math>L_2, R_1, R_2, \text{ and } R_3</math> all equal to <math>\R.</math> Then <math>{\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in I}}L_i = \R^2 \times \R</math> and <math>{\textstyle\prod\limits_{j \in J}} R_j = \R \times \R \times \R,</math> which can both be identified as the same set via the bijection that sends <math>((x, y), z) \in \R^2 \times \R</math> to <math>(x, y, z) \in \R \times \R \times \R.</math> Under this identification, <math>\left({\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in I}} L_i\right) \cap \, {\textstyle\prod\limits_{j \in J}} R_j ~=~ \R^3.</math>

====Binary {{math|⨯}} distributes over arbitrary {{math|⋃}} and {{math|⋂}}====

The binary [[Cartesian product]] ⨯ [[#Distributivity|distributes over]] arbitrary intersections (when the indexing set is not empty) and over arbitrary unions:

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{5}
L \times   \left(\bigcup_{i \in I} R_i\right) &\;=\;\;&& \bigcup_{i \in I} (L \times R_i) \qquad
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
L \times   \left(\bigcap_{i \in I} R_i\right) &\;=\;\;&& \bigcap_{i \in I} (L \times R_i) \qquad
&&\text{ (Left-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\bigcap_{i \in I}\, \text{ when } I \neq \varnothing\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right) \times R &\;=\;\;&& \bigcup_{i \in I} (L_i \times R) \qquad
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\cup\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right) \times R &\;=\;\;&& \bigcap_{i \in I} (L_i \times R) \qquad
&&\text{ (Right-distributivity of } \,\times\, \text{ over } \,\bigcap_{i \in I}\, \text{ when } I \neq \varnothing\, \text{)} \\[1.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

====Distributing arbitrary {{math|Π}} over arbitrary {{math|⋃}}{{anchor|Correctly distributing arbitrary Cartesian products over arbitrary unions}}====

Suppose that for each <math>i \in I,</math> <math>J_i</math> is a non-empty index set and for each <math>j \in J_i,</math> let <math>T_{i,j}</math> be any set (for example, to apply this law to <math>\left(S_{i,j}\right)_{(i, j) \in I \times J},</math> use <math>J_i \colon= J</math> for all <math>i \in I</math> and use <math>T_{i,j} \colon= S_{i,j}</math> for all <math>i \in I</math> and all <math>j \in J_i = J</math>). Let
<math display=block>{\textstyle \prod} J_{\bull} ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \prod_{i \in I} J_i</math> 
denote the [[Cartesian product]], which (as [[#Correctly distributing arbitrary intersections and arbitrary unions|mentioned above]]) can be interpreted as the set of all functions <math>f ~:~ I ~\to~ {\textstyle\bigcup\limits_{i \in I}} J_i</math> such that <math>f(i) \in J_i</math> for every <math>i \in I</math>.
Then 
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>\prod_{i \in I} \left[\;\bigcup_{j \in J_i} T_{i,j}\right] = \bigcup_{f \in \prod J_{\bull}} \left[\;\prod_{i \in I} T_{i,f(i)}\right]</math>|{{EquationRef|11|2=Eq. 11 Π∪ to ∪Π}}|LnSty=1px dashed black}}

where <math>{\textstyle \prod} J_{\bull} ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ {\textstyle\prod\limits_{i \in I}} J_i.</math>

====Unions {{math|⋃}} of {{math|Π}}====

For unions, only the following is guaranteed in general:
<math display=block>\bigcup_{j \in J} \; \prod_{i \in I} S_{i,j} ~~\color{Red}{\subseteq}\color{Black}{}~~ \prod_{i \in I} \; \bigcup_{j \in J} S_{i,j} \qquad \text{ and } \qquad \bigcup_{i \in I} \; \prod_{j \in J} S_{i,j} ~~\color{Red}{\subseteq}\color{Black}{}~~ \prod_{j \in J} \; \bigcup_{i \in I} S_{i,j}</math>
where <math>\left(S_{i,j}\right)_{(i,j) \in I \times J}</math> is a family of sets. 

* '''Example where equality fails''': Let <math>I = J = \{1, 2\},</math> let <math>S_{1,1} = S_{2,2} = \varnothing,</math> let <math>X \neq \varnothing,</math> and let <math>S_{1,2} = S_{2,1} = X.</math> Then <math display=block>\varnothing = \varnothing \cup \varnothing = \left(\prod_{i \in I} S_{i,1}\right) \cup \left(\prod_{i \in I} S_{i,2}\right) = \bigcup_{j \in J} \; \prod_{i \in I} S_{i,j} ~~\color{Red}{\neq}\color{Black}{}~~ \prod_{i \in I} \; \bigcup_{j \in J} S_{i,j} = \left(\bigcup_{j \in J} S_{1,j}\right) \times \left(\bigcup_{j \in J} S_{2,j}\right) = X \times X.</math> More generally, <math display=inline>\varnothing = \bigcup_{j \in J} \; \prod_{i \in I} S_{i,j}</math> if and only if for each <math>j \in J,</math> at least one of the sets in the <math>I</math>-indexed collections of sets <math>S_{\bullet,j} = \left(S_{i,j}\right)_{i\in I}</math> is empty, while <math display=inline>\prod_{i \in I} \; \bigcup_{j \in J} S_{i,j} \neq \varnothing</math> if and only if for each <math>i \in I,</math> at least one of the sets in the <math>J</math>-indexed collections of sets <math>S_{i,\bullet} = \left(S_{i,j}\right)_{j\in J}</math> is not empty.

However, 
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
\left(L \times R\right) ~\cup~ \left(L_2 \times R_2\right) 
~&=~ \left[\left(L \setminus L_2\right) \times R\right] ~\cup~ \left[\left(L_2 \setminus L\right) \times R_2\right] ~\cup~ \left[\left(L \cap L_2\right) \times \left(R \cup R_2\right)\right] \\[0.5ex]
~&=~ \left[L \times \left(R \setminus R_2\right)\right] ~\cup~ \left[L_2 \times \left(R_2 \setminus R\right)\right] ~\cup~ \left[\left(L \cup L_2\right) \times \left(R \cap R_2\right)\right] \\
\end{alignat}</math>

====Difference {{math|\}} of {{math|Π}}====

If <math>\left(L_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> and <math>\left(R_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> are two families of sets then:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
\left(\prod_{i \in I} L_i\right) ~\setminus~ \prod_{i \in I}R_i
~&=~ \;~ \bigcup_{j \in I} \; ~ \prod_{i \in I} \begin{cases}L_j \,\setminus\, R_j & \text{ if } i = j \\ L_i & \text{ if } i \neq j \\ \end{cases} \\[0.5ex]
~&=~ \;~ \bigcup_{j \in I} \; ~ \Big[\left(L_j \,\setminus\, R_j\right) ~\times~ \prod_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \neq i}} L_i\Big] \\[0.5ex]
~&=~ \bigcup_{\stackrel{j \in I,}{L_j \not\subseteq R_j}} \Big[\left(L_j \,\setminus\, R_j\right) ~\times~ \prod_{\stackrel{i \in I,}{j \neq i}} L_i\Big] \\[0.3ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
so for instance,
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
\left(L \times R\right) ~\setminus~ \left(L_2 \times R_2\right) 
~&=~ \left[\left(L \,\setminus\, L_2\right) \times R\right] ~\cup~ \left[L \times \left(R \,\setminus\, R_2\right)\right] \\
\end{alignat}</math>
and 
<math display=block>(L \times M \times R) ~\setminus~ \left(L_2 \times M_2 \times R_2\right) 
~=~ \left[\left(L \,\setminus\, L_2\right) \times M \times R\right] ~\cup~ \left[L \times \left(M \,\setminus\, M_2\right) \times R\right] ~\cup~ \left[L \times M \times \left(R \,\setminus\, R_2\right)\right]</math>

====Symmetric difference {{math|∆}} of {{math|Π}}====

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
\left(\prod_{i \in I} L_i\right) ~\triangle~ \left(\prod_{i \in I} R_i\right)
~&=~ \;~ \left(\prod_{i \in I} L_i\right) ~\cup~ \left(\prod_{i \in I} R_i\right) \;\setminus\; \prod_{i \in I} L_i \cap R_i \\[0.5ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

==Functions and sets==
{{See also|Image (mathematics)#Properties}}

Let <math>f : X \to Y</math> be any function. 

Let <math>L \text{ and } R</math> be completely arbitrary sets. Assume <math>A \subseteq X \text{ and } C \subseteq Y.</math> 

===Definitions===

Let <math>f : X \to Y</math> be any function, where we denote its {{em|domain}} <math>X</math> by <math>\operatorname{domain} f</math> and denote its {{em|codomain}} <math>Y</math> by <math>\operatorname{codomain} f.</math> 

Many of the identities below do not actually require that the sets be somehow related to <math>f</math>'s domain or [[codomain]] (that is, to <math>X</math> or <math>Y</math>) so when some kind of relationship is necessary then it will be clearly indicated. 
Because of this, in this article, if <math>L</math> is declared to be "{{em|any set}}," and it is not indicated that <math>L</math> must be somehow related to <math>X</math> or <math>Y</math> (say for instance, that it be a subset <math>X</math> or <math>Y</math>) then it is meant that <math>L</math> is truly arbitrary.<ref group=note>So for instance, it's even possible that <math>L \cap (X \cup Y) = \varnothing,</math> or that <math>L \cap X \neq \varnothing</math> {{em|and}} <math>L \cap Y \neq \varnothing</math> (which happens, for instance, if <math>X = Y</math>), etc.</ref> 
This generality is useful in situations where <math>f : X \to Y</math> is a map between two subsets <math>X \subseteq U</math> and <math>Y \subseteq V</math> of some larger sets <math>U</math> and <math>V,</math> and where the set <math>L</math> might not be entirely contained in <math>X = \operatorname{domain} f</math> and/or <math>Y = \operatorname{codomain} f</math> (e.g. if all that is known about <math>L</math> is that <math>L \subseteq U</math>); in such a situation it may be useful to know what can and cannot be said about <math>f(L)</math> and/or <math>f^{-1}(L)</math> without having to introduce a (potentially unnecessary) intersection such as: <math>f(L \cap X)</math> and/or <math>f^{-1}(L \cap Y).</math>  

'''Images and preimages of sets'''

If <math>L</math> is {{em|any}} set then the {{em|[[Image (mathematics)|{{em|image}}]] of <math>L</math> under <math>f</math>}} is defined to be the set: 
<math display=block>f(L) ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{\,f(l) ~:~ l \in L \cap \operatorname{domain} f\,\}</math>
while the {{em|[[preimage]] of <math>L</math> under <math>f</math>}} is: 
<math display=block>f^{-1}(L) ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \{\,x \in \operatorname{domain} f ~:~ f(x) \in L\,\}</math>
where if <math>L = \{s\}</math> is a singleton set then the {{em|[[Fiber (mathematics)|fiber]]}} or {{em|[[preimage]] of <math>s</math> under <math>f</math>}} is
<math display=block>f^{-1}(s) ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ f^{-1}(\{s\}) ~=~ \{\,x \in \operatorname{domain} f ~:~ f(x) = s\,\}.</math>

Denote by <math>\operatorname{Im} f</math> or <math>\operatorname{image} f</math> the {{em|image}} or {{em|[[Range of a function|range]]}} of <math>f : X \to Y,</math> which is the set: 
<math display=block>\operatorname{Im} f ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ f(X) ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ f(\operatorname{domain} f) ~=~ \{f(x) ~:~ x \in \operatorname{domain} f\}.</math>

'''Saturated sets'''

{{Main|Saturated set}}

A set <math>A</math> is said to be {{em|<math>f</math>-'''saturated'''}} or a '''{{em|[[saturated set|{{visible anchor|saturated set}}]]}}''' if any of the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}  
<ol>
<li>There exists a set <math>R</math> such that <math>A = f^{-1}(R).</math>
* Any such set <math>R</math> necessarily contains <math>f(A)</math> as a subset.
* Any set not entirely contained in the domain of <math>f</math> cannot be <math>f</math>-saturated.</li>
<li><math>A = f^{-1}(f(A)).</math></li>
<li><math>A \supseteq f^{-1}(f(A))</math> and <math>A \subseteq \operatorname{domain} f.</math>
* The inclusion <math>L \cap \operatorname{domain} f \subseteq f^{-1}(f(L))</math> always holds, where if <math>A \subseteq \operatorname{domain} f</math> then this becomes <math>A \subseteq f^{-1}(f(A)).</math></li>
<li><math>A \subseteq \operatorname{domain} f</math> and if <math>a \in A</math> and <math>x \in \operatorname{domain} f</math> satisfy <math>f(x) = f(a),</math> then <math>x \in A.</math>
<li>Whenever a fiber of <math>f</math> intersects <math>A,</math> then <math>A</math> contains the entire fiber. In other words, <math>A</math> contains every <math>f</math>-fiber that intersects it.</li>
* Explicitly: whenever <math>y \in \operatorname{Im} f</math> is such that <math>A \cap f^{-1}(y) \neq \varnothing,</math> then <math>f^{-1}(y) \subseteq A.</math>
* In both this statement and the next, the set <math>\operatorname{Im} f</math> may be replaced with any superset of <math>\operatorname{Im} f</math> (such as <math>\operatorname{codomain} f</math>) and the resulting statement will still be equivalent to the rest.
<li>The intersection of <math>A</math> with a fiber of <math>f</math> is equal to the empty set or to the fiber itself. 
* Explicitly: for every <math>y \in \operatorname{Im} f,</math> the intersection <math>A \cap f^{-1}(y)</math> is equal to the [[empty set]] <math>\varnothing</math> or to <math>f^{-1}(y)</math> (that is, <math>A \cap f^{-1}(y) = \varnothing</math> or <math>A \cap f^{-1}(y) = f^{-1}(y)</math>). 
</li>
</ol>
For a set <math>A</math> to be <math>f</math>-saturated, it is necessary that <math>A \subseteq \operatorname{domain} f.</math> 

'''Compositions and restrictions of functions'''

If <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are maps then <math>g \circ f</math> denotes the {{em|[[Function composition|composition]]}} map 
<math display=block>g \circ f ~:~ \{\,x \in \operatorname{domain} f ~:~ f(x) \in \operatorname{domain} g\,\} ~\to~ \operatorname{codomain} g</math>
with domain and codomain
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
\operatorname{domain}   (g \circ f) &= \{\,x \in \operatorname{domain} f ~:~ f(x) \in \operatorname{domain}  g\,\} \\[0.4ex]
\operatorname{codomain} (g \circ f) &= \operatorname{codomain} g \\[0.7ex]
\end{alignat}</math> 
defined by
<math display=block>(g \circ f)(x) ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ g(f(x)).</math>

The {{em|[[Restriction (mathematics)|restriction]] of <math>f : X \to Y</math> to <math>L,</math>}} denoted by <math>f\big\vert_L,</math> is the map 
<math display=block>f\big\vert_L ~:~ L \cap \operatorname{domain} f ~\to~ Y</math>
with <math>\operatorname{domain} f\big\vert_L ~=~ L \cap \operatorname{domain} f</math> defined by sending <math>x \in L \cap \operatorname{domain} f</math> to <math>f(x);</math> that is, 
<math display=block>f\big\vert_L(x) ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ f (x).</math> 
Alternatively, <math>~f\big\vert_L ~=~ f \circ \operatorname{In}~</math> where <math>~\operatorname{In} ~:~ L \cap X \to X~</math> denotes the [[inclusion map]], which is defined by <math>\operatorname{In}(s) ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ s.</math>

===(Pre)Images of arbitrary unions ⋃'s and intersections ⋂'s===

If <math>\left(L_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> is a family of arbitrary sets indexed by <math>I \neq \varnothing</math> then:{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=102-120}}
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right)       \;&~\;\color{Red}{\subseteq}\color{Black}{}~ \;\;\;\bigcap_{i \in I} f\left(L_i\right) \\
f\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right)       \;&~=~ \;\bigcup_{i \in I} f\left(L_i\right) \\
f^{-1}\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} L_i\right)  \;&~=~ \;\bigcup_{i \in I} f^{-1}\left(L_i\right) \\
f^{-1}\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right)  \;&~=~ \;\bigcap_{i \in I} f^{-1}\left(L_i\right) \\
\end{alignat}</math>

So of these four identities, it is {{em|<u>only</u>}} '''{{em|images of intersections}}''' that are not always preserved. Preimages preserve all basic set operations. Unions are preserved by both images and preimages. 

If all <math>L_i</math> are <math>f</math>-saturated then <math>\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i</math> be will be <math>f</math>-saturated and equality will hold in the first relation above; explicitly, this means: 
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>f\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} L_i\right)  ~=~  \bigcap_{i \in I} f\left(L_i\right) \qquad \textit{IF} \qquad X \cap L_i = f^{-1}\left(f\left(L_i\right)\right) \quad \text{ for all } \quad i \in I.</math>|{{EquationRef|Conditional Equality 10a}}}}

If <math>\left(A_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> is a family of arbitrary subsets of <math>X = \operatorname{domain} f,</math> which means that <math>A_i \subseteq X</math> for all <math>i,</math> then {{EquationNote|Conditional Equality 10a}} becomes:
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>f\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i\right)  ~=~  \bigcap_{i \in I} f\left(A_i\right) \qquad \textit{IF} \qquad A_i = f^{-1}\left(f\left(A_i\right)\right) \quad \text{ for all } \quad i \in I.</math>|{{EquationRef|Conditional Equality 10b}}}}

===(Pre)Images of binary set operations===

Throughout, let <math>L</math> and <math>R</math> be any sets and let <math>f : X \to Y</math> be any function.

'''Summary'''

As the table below shows, set equality is {{em|not}} guaranteed {{em|only}} for {{em|images}} of: intersections, set subtractions, and symmetric differences. 

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Image
! Preimage
! {{nowrap|Additional assumptions on sets}}

|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>\,~~~~f(L \cup R) ~=~ f(L) \cup f(R)</math><ref name="kelley-1985">{{harvnb|Kelley|1985|p=[{{Google books|plainurl=y|id=-goleb9Ov3oC|page=85|text=The image of the union of a family of subsets of X is the union of the images, but, in general, the image of the intersection is not the intersection of the images}} 85]}}</ref>
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f^{-1}(L \cup R) ~=~ f^{-1}(L) \cup f^{-1}(R)</math>{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}
|None
|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math display=block>f(L \cap R) ~\subseteq~ f(L) \cap f(R)</math>
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f^{-1}(L \cap R) ~=~ f^{-1}(L) \cap f^{-1}(R)</math>{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}
|None
|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math display=block>f(L \setminus R) ~\supseteq~ f(L) \setminus f(R)</math>
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>\begin{alignat}{4}
f^{-1}(L) \setminus f^{-1}(R) 
&= f^{-1}&&( &&L                           &&\setminus  &&R) \\
&= f^{-1}&&( &&L                           &&\setminus [&&R \cap \operatorname{Im} f]) \\
&= f^{-1}&&([&&L \cap \operatorname{Im} f] &&\setminus  &&R) \\
&= f^{-1}&&([&&L \cap \operatorname{Im} f] &&\setminus [&&R \cap \operatorname{Im} f]) 
\end{alignat}</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=102-120}}{{sfn|Monk|1969|pp=24-54}}
|None
|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math display=block>f(X \setminus R) ~\supseteq~ f(X) \setminus f(R)</math>
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>\begin{alignat}{4}
X \setminus f^{-1}(R) 
&= f^{-1}(&&Y                   &&\setminus  &&R) \\
&= f^{-1}(&&Y                   &&\setminus [&&R \cap \operatorname{Im} f]) \\
&= f^{-1}(&&\operatorname{Im} f &&\setminus  &&R) \\
&= f^{-1}(&&\operatorname{Im} f &&\setminus [&&R \cap \operatorname{Im} f]) 
\end{alignat}</math><ref group=note>The conclusion <math>X \setminus f^{-1}(R) = f^{-1}(Y \setminus R)</math> can also be written as: <math>f^{-1}(R)^\complement ~=~ f^{-1}\left(R^\complement\right).</math></ref>
|None

|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f^{-1}\left(L ~\triangle~ R\right) ~=~ f^{-1}(L) ~\triangle~ f^{-1}(R)</math>
|None
|}

'''Preimages preserve set operations'''

Preimages of sets are well-behaved with respect to all basic set operations:

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f^{-1}(L \cup R) ~&=~ f^{-1}(L) \cup f^{-1}(R) \\
f^{-1}(L \cap R) ~&=~ f^{-1}(L) \cap f^{-1}(R) \\
f^{-1}(L \setminus\, R) ~&=~ f^{-1}(L) \setminus\, f^{-1}(R) \\
f^{-1}(L \,\triangle\, R) ~&=~ f^{-1}(L) \,\triangle\, f^{-1}(R) \\
\end{alignat}</math>

In words, preimages [[Distributive property|distribute over]] unions, intersections, set subtraction, and symmetric difference. 

'''Images {{em|only}} preserve unions'''

Images of unions are well-behaved:

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f(L \cup R) ~&=~ f(L) \cup f(R) \\
\end{alignat}</math>

but images of the other basic set operations are {{em|not}} since only the following are guaranteed in general:

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f(L \cap R) ~&\subseteq~ f(L) \cap f(R) \\
f(L \setminus R) ~&\supseteq~ f(L) \setminus f(R) \\
f(L \triangle R) ~&\supseteq~ f(L) \,\triangle\, f(R) \\
\end{alignat}</math>

In words, images [[Distributive property|distribute over]] unions but not necessarily over intersections, set subtraction, or symmetric difference. What these latter three operations have in common is set subtraction: they either {{em|are}} [[set subtraction]] <math>L \setminus R</math> or else they can naturally {{em|be defined}} as the set subtraction of two sets: 
<math display=block>L \cap R = L \setminus (L \setminus R) \quad \text{ and } \quad L \triangle R = (L \cup R) \setminus (L \cap R).</math> 

If <math>L = X</math> then <math>f(X \setminus R) \supseteq f(X) \setminus f(R)</math> where as in the more general case, equality is not guaranteed. If <math>f</math> is surjective then <math>f(X \setminus R) ~\supseteq~ Y \setminus f(R),</math> which can be rewritten as: <math>f\left(R^\complement\right) ~\supseteq~ f(R)^\complement</math> if <math>R^\complement ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ X \setminus R</math> and <math>f(R)^\complement ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ Y \setminus f(R).</math>

====Counter-examples: images of operations not distributing====

[[File:Image preimage conterexample intersection.gif|thumb|right|upright=1.6|Picture showing <math>f</math> failing to [[Distributive property|distribute over set intersection]]:<br/>
{{center|<math>f\left(A_1 \cap A_2\right) \subsetneq f\left(A_1\right) \cap f\left(A_2\right).</math>}}
The map <math>f : \R \to \R</math> is defined by <math>x \mapsto x^2,</math> where <math>\R</math> denotes the [[real number]]s. The sets <math>A_1 = [-4, 2]</math> and <math>A_2 = [-2, 4]</math> are shown in {{color|blue|blue}} immediately below the <math>x</math>-axis while their intersection <math>A_3 = [-2, 2]</math> is shown in {{color|green|green}}.]]

If <math>f : \{1, 2\} \to Y</math> is constant, <math>L = \{1\},</math> and <math>R = \{2\}</math> then all four of the set containments
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f(L \cap R) ~&\subsetneq~ f(L) \cap f(R) \\
f(L \setminus R) ~&\supsetneq~ f(L) \setminus f(R) \\
f(X \setminus R) ~&\supsetneq~ f(X) \setminus f(R) \\
f(L \triangle R) ~&\supsetneq~ f(L) \triangle f(R) \\
\end{alignat}</math>
are [[Proper subset|strict/proper]] (that is, the sets are not equal) since one side is the empty set while the other is non-empty. Thus equality is not guaranteed for even the simplest of functions. 
The example above is now generalized to show that these four set equalities can fail for any [[constant function]] whose domain contains at least two (distinct) points. 

'''{{em|Example}}''':{{anchor|ConstantFunctionWithDisjointSubsetsExample}} Let <math>f : X \to Y</math> be any constant function with image <math>f(X) = \{y\}</math> and suppose that <math>L, R \subseteq X</math> are non-empty disjoint subsets; that is, <math>L \neq \varnothing, R \neq \varnothing,</math> and <math>L \cap R = \varnothing,</math> which implies that all of the sets <math>L ~\triangle~ R = L \cup R,</math> <math>\,L \setminus R = L,</math> and <math>X \setminus R \supseteq L \setminus R</math> are not empty and so consequently, their images under <math>f</math> are all equal to <math>\{y\}.</math> 

<ol>
<li>The containment <math>~f(L \setminus R) ~\supsetneq~ f(L) \setminus f(R)~</math> is strict: <math display=block>\{y\} ~=~ f(L \setminus R) ~\neq~ f(L) \setminus f(R) ~=~ \{y\} \setminus \{y\} ~=~ \varnothing</math>
In words: functions might not [[Distributive property|distribute over set subtraction <math>\,\setminus\,</math>]] 
</li>
<li>The containment <math>~f(X \setminus R) ~\supsetneq~ f(X) \setminus f(R)~</math> is strict: <math display=block>\{y\} ~=~ f(X \setminus R) ~\neq~ f(X) \setminus f(R) ~=~ \{y\} \setminus \{y\} ~=~ \varnothing.</math>
</li>
<li>The containment <math>~f(L ~\triangle~ R) ~\supsetneq~ f(L) ~\triangle~ f(R)~</math> is strict: <math display=block>\{y\} ~=~ f\left(L ~\triangle~ R\right) ~\neq~ f(L) ~\triangle~ f(R) ~=~ \{y\} \triangle \{y\} ~=~ \varnothing</math>
In words: functions might not [[Distributive property|distribute over symmetric difference <math>\,\triangle\,</math>]] (which can be defined as the set subtraction of two sets: <math>L \triangle R = (L \cup R) \setminus (L \cap R)</math>).
</li>
<li>The containment <math>~f(L \cap R) ~\subsetneq~ f(L) \cap f(R)~</math> is strict: <math display=block>\varnothing ~=~ f(\varnothing) ~=~ f(L \cap R) ~\neq~ f(L) \cap f(R) ~=~ \{y\} \cap \{y\} ~=~ \{y\}</math>
In words: functions might not [[Distributive property|distribute over set intersection <math>\,\cap\,</math>]] (which can be defined as the set subtraction of two sets: <math>L \cap R = L \setminus (L \setminus R)</math>).
</li>
</ol>

What the set operations in these four examples have in common is that they either {{em|are}} [[set subtraction]] <math>\setminus</math> (examples (1) and (2)) or else they can naturally {{em|be defined}} as the set subtraction of two sets (examples (3) and (4)).

'''Mnemonic''': In fact, for each of the above four set formulas for which equality is not guaranteed, the direction of the containment (that is, whether to use <math>\,\subseteq \text{ or } \supseteq\,</math>) can always be deduced by imagining the function <math>f</math> as being {{em|constant}} and the two sets (<math>L</math> and <math>R</math>) as being non-empty disjoint subsets of its domain. This is because {{em|every}} equality fails for such a function and sets: one side will be always be <math>\varnothing</math> and the other non-empty − from this fact, the correct choice of <math>\,\subseteq \text{ or } \supseteq\,</math> can be deduced by answering: "which side is empty?" For example, to decide if the <math>?</math> in 
<math display=block>f(L \triangle R) \setminus f(R) ~\;~?~\;~ f((L \triangle R) \setminus R)</math>
should be <math>\,\subseteq \text{ or } \supseteq,\,</math> pretend<ref group=note>Whether or not it is even feasible for the function <math>f</math> to be constant and the sets <math>L \triangle R</math> and <math>R</math> to be non-empty and disjoint is irrelevant for reaching the correct conclusion about whether to use <math>\,\subseteq \text{ or } \supseteq.\,</math></ref> 
that <math>f</math> is constant and that <math>L \triangle R</math> and <math>R</math> are non-empty disjoint subsets of <math>f</math>'s domain; then the {{em|left}} hand side would be empty (since <math>f(L \triangle R) \setminus f(R) = \{f\text{'s single value}\} \setminus \{f\text{'s single value}\} = \varnothing</math>), which indicates that <math>\,?\,</math> should be <math>\,\subseteq\,</math> (the resulting statement is always guaranteed to be true) because this is the choice that will make
<math display=block>\varnothing = \text{left hand side} ~\;~?~\;~ \text{right hand side}</math>
true. 
Alternatively, the correct direction of containment can also be deduced by consideration of any constant <math>f : \{1, 2\} \to Y</math> with <math>L = \{1\}</math> and <math>R = \{2\}.</math> 

Furthermore, this mnemonic can also be used to correctly deduce whether or not a set operation always distribute over images or preimages; for example, to determine whether or not <math>f(L \cap R)</math> always equals <math>f(L) \cap f(R),</math> or alternatively, whether or not <math>f^{-1}(L \cap R)</math> always equals <math>f^{-1}(L) \cap f^{-1}(R)</math> (although <math>\,\cap\,</math> was used here, it can replaced by <math>\,\cup, \,\setminus, \text{ or } \,\triangle</math>). The answer to such a question can, as before, be deduced by consideration of this constant function: the answer for the general case (that is, for arbitrary <math>f, L,</math> and <math>R</math>) is always the same as the answer for this choice of (constant) function and disjoint non-empty sets.

====Conditions guaranteeing that images distribute over set operations====

'''Characterizations of when equality holds for {{em|all}} sets''':

For any function <math>f : X \to Y,</math> the following statements are equivalent:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f : X \to Y</math> is [[Injective function|injective]]. 
* This means: <math>f(x) \neq f(y)</math> for all distinct <math>x, y \in X.</math>
</li>
<li><math>f(L \cap R) = f(L) \,\cap\, f(R) \, \text{ for all } \, L, R \subseteq X.</math> (The equals sign <math>\,=\,</math> can be replaced with <math>\,\supseteq\,</math>).
</li>
<li><math>f(L \,\setminus R) = f(L) \,\setminus\, f(R) \; \text{ for all } \, L, R \subseteq X.</math> (The equals sign <math>\,=\,</math> can be replaced with <math>\,\subseteq\,</math>).
</li>
<li><math>f(X \setminus R) = f(X) \setminus\, f(R) \; \text{ for all } \, ~~~~~R \subseteq X.</math> (The equals sign <math>\,=\,</math> can be replaced with <math>\,\subseteq\,</math>).
</li>
<li><math>f(L \,\triangle\, R) = f(L) \,\triangle\, f(R) \; \text{ for all } \, L, R \subseteq X.</math> (The equals sign <math>\,=\,</math> can be replaced with <math>\,\subseteq\,</math>).
</li>
<li>Any one of the four statements (b) - (e) but with the words "for all" replaced with any one of the following:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li>"for all [[Singleton set|singleton subsets]]"
* In particular, the statement that results from (d) gives a characterization of injectivity that explicitly involves only one point (rather than two): <math>f</math> is injective if and only if <math>f(x) \not\in f(X \setminus \{x\}) \; \text{ for every } \, x \in X.</math></li>
<li>"for all [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] singleton subsets"
* For statement (d), this is the same as: "for all singleton subsets" (because the definition of "[[pairwise disjoint]]" is satisfies vacuously by any family that consists of exactly 1 set).</li>
<li>"for all disjoint subsets"</li>
</ol>
</li>
</ol>

In particular, if a map is not known to be injective then barring additional information, there is no guarantee that any of the equalities in statements (b) - (e) hold.

[[#ConstantFunctionWithDisjointSubsetsExample|An example above]] can be used to help prove this characterization. Indeed, comparison of that example with such a proof suggests that the example is representative of the fundamental reason why one of these four equalities in statements (b) - (e) might not hold (that is, representative of "what goes wrong" when a set equality does not hold).

=====Conditions for f(L⋂R) = f(L)⋂f(R){{anchor|Image of an intersection ⋂|Image of an intersection}}=====

<math display=block>f(L \cap R) ~\subseteq~ f(L) \cap f(R) \qquad\qquad \text{ always holds}</math>

''Characterizations of equality'': The following statements are equivalent:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f(L \cap R) ~=~ f(L) \cap f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(L \cap R) ~\supseteq~ f(L) \cap f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R)) ~\subseteq~ f^{-1}(f(L \cap R))</math>
* The left hand side <math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R))</math> is always equal to <math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(L) \cap f(R))</math> (because <math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R)) ~\subseteq~ f^{-1}(f(L))</math> always holds).</li>
<li><math>R \cap f^{-1}(f(L)) ~\subseteq~ f^{-1}(f(L \cap R))</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R)) ~=~ f^{-1}(f(L \cap R)) \cap L</math></li>
<li><math>R \cap f^{-1}(f(L)) ~=~ f^{-1}(f(L \cap R)) \cap R</math></li>
<li>If <math>l \in L</math> satisfies <math>f(l) \in f(R)</math> then <math>f(l) \in f(L \cap R).</math></li>
<li>If <math>y \in f(L)</math> but <math>y \notin f(L \cap R)</math> then <math>y \notin f(R).</math></li>
<li><math>f(L) \, \setminus \, f(L \cap R) ~\subseteq~ f(L) \, \setminus \, f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(R) \, \setminus \, f(L \cap R) ~\subseteq~ f(R) \, \setminus \, f(L)</math></li>
<li><math>f(L \cup R) \setminus f(L \cap R) ~\subseteq~ f(L) \,\triangle\, f(R)</math></li>
<li>Any of the above three conditions (i) - (k) but with the subset symbol <math>\,\subseteq\,</math> replaced with an equals sign <math>\,=.\,</math></li>
</ol>

''Sufficient conditions for equality'': Equality holds if any of the following are true:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f</math> is injective.<ref name="munkres-2000-p21">See {{harvnb|Munkres|2000|p=21}}</ref></li>
<li>The restriction <math>f\big\vert_{L \cup R}</math> is injective.</li>
<li><math>f^{-1}(f(R)) ~\subseteq~ R</math><ref group=note name="Depends only on R"/></li>
<li><math>f^{-1}(f(L)) ~\subseteq~ L</math>
<!--This is equivalent to: <li><math>R \cap \operatorname{domain} f ~=~ f^{-1}(f(R))</math><ref group=note name="Depends only on R"/> &nbsp;or<br/><math>L \cap \operatorname{domain} f ~=~ f^{-1}(f(L))</math></li>--></li>
<li><math>R</math> is <math>f</math>-saturated; that is, <math>f^{-1}(f(R)) = R</math><ref group=note name="Depends only on R"/></li>
<li><math>L</math> is <math>f</math>-saturated; that is, <math>f^{-1}(f(L)) = L</math></li>
<li><math>f(L) ~\subseteq~ f(L \cap R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(R) ~\subseteq~ f(L \cap R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(L \,\setminus\, R) ~\subseteq~ f(L) \setminus \, f(R)</math> or equivalently, <math>f(L \,\setminus\, R) ~=~ f(L) \setminus f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(R \,\setminus\, L) ~\subseteq~ f(R) \setminus \, f(L)</math> or equivalently, <math>f(R \,\setminus\, L) ~=~ f(R) \setminus f(L)</math></li>
<li><math>f\left(L ~\triangle~ R\right) \subseteq f(L) ~\triangle~ f(R)</math> or equivalently, <math>f\left(L ~\triangle~ R\right) = f(L) ~\triangle~ f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>R \cap \operatorname{domain} f \,\subseteq L</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap \operatorname{domain} f \,\subseteq R</math></li>
<li><math>R \subseteq L</math></li>
<li><math>L \subseteq R</math></li>
</ol>

In addition, the following always hold:
<math display=block>f\left(f^{-1}(L) \cap R\right) ~=~ L \cap f(R)</math>
<math display=block>f\left(f^{-1}(L) \cup R\right) ~=~ (L \cap \operatorname{Im} f) \cup f(R)</math>

=====Conditions for f(L\R) = f(L)\f(R){{anchor|Image of a set subtraction \|Image of a set subtraction}}=====

<math display=block>f(L \setminus R) ~\supseteq~ f(L) \setminus f(R) \qquad\qquad \text{ always holds}</math>

''Characterizations of equality'': The following statements are equivalent:<ref group=proof name=proofCharOfPullingLminusR />
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f(L \setminus R) ~=~ f(L) \setminus f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(L \setminus R) ~\subseteq~ f(L) \setminus f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R)) ~\subseteq~ R</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R)) ~=~ L \cap R \cap \operatorname{domain} f</math></li>
<li>Whenever <math>y \in f(L) \cap f(R)</math> then <math>L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R.</math></li>
<li><math display=inline>f(L) \cap f(R) ~\subseteq~ \left\{y \in f(L) : L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R\right\}</math>
* The set on the right hand side is always equal to <math>\left\{y \in f(L \cap R) :  L \cap f^{-1}(y) \,\subseteq R\right\}.</math></li>
<li><math display=inline>f(L) \cap f(R) ~=~ \left\{y \in f(L) : L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R\right\}</math>
* This is the above condition (f) but with the subset symbol <math>\,\subseteq\,</math> replaced with an equals sign <math>\,=.\,</math></li>
</ol>

''Necessary conditions for equality'' (excluding characterizations):  If equality holds then the following are necessarily true:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f(L \cap R) = f(L) \cap f(R),</math> or equivalently <math>f(L \cap R) \supseteq f(L) \cap f(R).</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R)) ~=~ L \cap f^{-1}(f(L \cap R))</math> or equivalently, <math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R)) ~\subseteq~ f^{-1}(f(L \cap R))</math></li>
<li><math>R \cap f^{-1}(f(L)) ~=~ R \cap f^{-1}(f(L \cap R))</math></li>
</ol>

''Sufficient conditions for equality'': Equality holds if any of the following are true:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f</math> is injective.</li>
<li>The restriction <math>f\big\vert_{L \cup R}</math> is injective.</li>
<li><math>f^{-1}(f(R)) ~\subseteq~ R</math><ref group=note name="Depends only on R">Note that this condition depends entirely on <math>R</math> and {{em|not}} on <math>L.</math></ref> or equivalently, <math>R \cap \operatorname{domain} f ~=~ f^{-1}(f(R))</math></li>
<li><math>R</math> is <math>f</math>-saturated; that is, <math>R = f^{-1}(f(R)).</math><ref group=note name="Depends only on R"/></li>
<li><math>f\left(L ~\triangle~ R\right) \subseteq f(L) ~\triangle~ f(R)</math> or equivalently, <math>f\left(L ~\triangle~ R\right) = f(L) ~\triangle~ f(R)</math></li>
</ol>

=====Conditions for f(X\R) = f(X)\f(R){{anchor|Image of a set subtracted from the domain \|Image of a set subtracted from the domain}}=====

<math display=block>f(X \setminus R) ~\supseteq~ f(X) \setminus f(R) \qquad\qquad \text{ always holds, where } f : X \to Y</math>

''Characterizations of equality'': The following statements are equivalent:<ref group=proof name=proofCharOfPullingLminusR />
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f(X \setminus R) ~=~ f(X) \setminus f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(X \setminus R) ~\subseteq~ f(X) \setminus f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f^{-1}(f(R)) \,\subseteq\, R</math></li>
<li><math>f^{-1}(f(R)) \,=\, R \cap \operatorname{domain} f</math></li>
<li><math>R \cap \operatorname{domain} f</math> is <math>f</math>-saturated.</li>
<li>Whenever <math>y \in f(R)</math> then <math>f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R.</math></li>
<li><math display=inline>f(R) ~\subseteq~ \left\{ y \in f(R) : f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\}</math></li>
<li><math display=inline>f(R) ~=~ \left\{ y \in f(R) : f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\}</math></li>
</ol>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;where if <math>R \subseteq \operatorname{domain} f</math> then this list can be extended to include:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;" start=9>
<li><math>R</math> is <math>f</math>-saturated; that is, <math>R = f^{-1}(f(R)).</math></li>
</ol>

''Sufficient conditions for equality'':  Equality holds if any of the following are true:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f</math> is injective.</li>
<li><math>R</math> is <math>f</math>-saturated; that is, <math>R = f^{-1}(f(R)).</math></li>
</ol>

=====Conditions for f(L∆R) = f(L)∆f(R){{anchor|Image of a symmetric difference ∆|Image of a symmetric difference}}=====

<math display=block>f\left(L ~\triangle~ R\right) ~\supseteq~ f(L) ~\triangle~ f(R) \qquad\qquad \text{ always holds}</math>

''Characterizations of equality'': The following statements are equivalent:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f\left(L ~\triangle~ R\right) = f(L) ~\triangle~ f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f\left(L ~\triangle~ R\right) \subseteq f(L) ~\triangle~ f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(L \,\setminus\, R) = f(L) \,\setminus\, f(R)</math> &nbsp;and&nbsp; <math>f(R \,\setminus\, L) = f(R) \,\setminus\, f(L)</math></li>
<li><math>f(L \,\setminus\, R) \subseteq f(L) \,\setminus\, f(R)</math> &nbsp;and&nbsp; <math>f(R \,\setminus\, L) \subseteq f(R) \,\setminus\, f(L)</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R)) ~\subseteq~ R</math> &nbsp;and&nbsp; <math>R \cap f^{-1}(f(L)) ~\subseteq~ L</math>
* The inclusions <math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R)) ~\subseteq~ f^{-1}(f(L))</math> and <math>R \cap f^{-1}(f(L)) ~\subseteq~ f^{-1}(f(R))</math> always hold.</li>
<li><math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(R)) ~=~ R \cap f^{-1}(f(L))</math>
* If this above set equality holds, then this set will also be equal to both <math>L \cap R \cap \operatorname{domain} f</math> and <math>L \cap R \cap f^{-1}(f(L \cap R)).</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(L \cap R)) ~=~ R \cap f^{-1}(f(L \cap R))</math> &nbsp;and&nbsp; <math>f(L \cap R) ~\supseteq~ f(L) \cap f(R).</math></li>
</ol>

''Necessary conditions for equality'' (excluding characterizations): If equality holds then the following are necessarily true:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f(L \cap R) = f(L) \cap f(R),</math> or equivalently <math>f(L \cap R) \supseteq f(L) \cap f(R).</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap f^{-1}(f(L \cap R)) ~=~ R \cap f^{-1}(f(L \cap R))</math></li>
</ol>

''Sufficient conditions for equality'': Equality holds if any of the following are true:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f</math> is injective.</li>
<li>The restriction <math>f\big\vert_{L \cup R}</math> is injective.</li>
</ol>

====Exact formulas/equalities for images of set operations====

=====Formulas for f(L\R) ={{anchor|Image of set subtraction|Formulas for the image of set subtraction}}=====

For any function <math>f : X \to Y</math> and any sets <math>L</math> and <math>R,</math><ref group=proof name=ProofImagesOfSetSubtractions>Let <math>P := \left\{y \in Y : L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R\right\}</math> and let <math>(\star)</math> denote the set equality <math>f(L \setminus R) = Y \setminus P,</math> which will now be proven. If <math>y \in Y \setminus P</math> then <math>L \cap f^{-1}(y) \not\subseteq R</math> so there exists some <math>x \in L \cap f^{-1}(y) \setminus R;</math> now <math>f^{-1}(y) \subseteq X</math> implies <math>x \in L \cap X \setminus R</math> so that <math>y = f(x) \in f(L \cap X \setminus R) = f(L \setminus R).</math> To prove the reverse inclusion <math>f(L \setminus R) \subseteq Y \setminus P,</math> let <math>y \in f(L \setminus R)</math> so that there exists some <math>x \in X \cap L \setminus R</math> such that <math>y = f(x).</math> Then <math>x \in L \cap f^{-1}(y) \setminus R</math> so that <math>L \cap f^{-1}(y) \not\subseteq R</math> and thus <math>y \not\in P,</math> which proves that <math>y \in Y \setminus P,</math> as desired. <math>\blacksquare</math> Defining <math>Q := f(L) \cap P = \left\{ y \in f(L) : L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\},</math> the identity <math>f(L \setminus R) = f(L) \setminus Q</math> follows from <math>(\star)</math> and the inclusions <math>f(L \setminus R) \subseteq f(L) \subseteq Y.</math> <math>\blacksquare</math></ref>
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f(L \setminus R)
&= Y ~~~\;\,\, \setminus \left\{ y \in Y ~~~~~~~~~~\;\,   ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= f(L)        \setminus \left\{ y \in f(L)~~~~~~~\,      ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= f(L)        \setminus \left\{ y \in f(L \cap R)        ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= f(L)        \setminus \left\{ y \in V~~~~~~~~~~~~\,    ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\} \qquad && \text{ for any superset } \quad V \supseteq f(L \cap R) \\[0.4ex]
&= f(S)        \setminus \left\{ y \in f(S)~~~~~~~\,      ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\} \qquad && \text{ for any superset } \quad S \supseteq L \cap X. \\[0.7ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

=====Formulas for f(X\R) ={{anchor|Image of set subtraction from the domain|Formulas for the image of set subtraction from the domain}}=====

Taking <math>L := X = \operatorname{domain} f</math> in the above formulas gives:
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f(X \setminus R)
&= Y ~~~\;\,\,            \setminus \left\{ y \in Y ~~~~\;\,\,           :~ f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= f(X)                   \setminus \left\{ y \in f(X) ~                 :~ f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= f(X)                   \setminus \left\{ y \in f(R) ~                 :~ f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= f(X)                   \setminus \left\{ y \in W ~~~\;\,\,            :~ f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\} \qquad \text{ for any superset } \quad W \supseteq f(R) \\[0.4ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
where the set <math>\left\{ y \in f(R) : f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\}</math> is equal to the image under <math>f</math> of the largest <math>f</math>-saturated subset of <math>R.</math>
<ul>
<li>In general, only <math>f(X \setminus R) \,\supseteq\, f(X) \setminus f(R)</math> always holds and equality is not guaranteed; but replacing "<math>f(R)</math>" with its subset "<math>\left\{ y \in f(R) : f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\}</math>" results in a formula in which equality is {{em|always}} guaranteed: 
<math display=block>f(X \setminus R) \,=\, f(X) \setminus  \left\{ y \in f(R) : f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\}.</math> 
From this it follows that:<ref group=proof name=proofCharOfPullingLminusR>Let <math>f_R := \left\{ y \in f(L) : L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\}</math> where because <math>f_R \subseteq f(R \cap L),</math> <math>f_R</math> is also equal to <math>f_R = \left\{ y \in f(R \cap L) : L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\}.</math> As proved above, <math>f(L \setminus R) = f(L) \setminus f_R</math> so that <math>f(L) \setminus f(R) = f(L \setminus R)</math> if and only if <math>f(L) \setminus f(R) = f(L) \setminus f_R.</math> Since <math>f(L) \setminus f(R) = f(L) \setminus (f(L) \cap f(R)),</math> this happens if and only if <math>f(L) \setminus (f(L) \cap f(R)) = f(L) \setminus f_R.</math> Because <math>f(L) \cap f(R) \text{ and } f_R</math> are both subsets of <math>f(L),</math> the condition on the right hand side happens if and only if <math>f(L) \cap f(R) = f_R.</math> Because <math>f_R \subseteq f(R \cap L) \subseteq f(L) \cap f(R),</math> the equality <math>f(L) \cap f(R) = f_R</math> holds if and only if <math>f(L) \cap f(R) \subseteq f_R.</math> <math>\blacksquare</math> If <math>f(R) \subseteq f(L)</math> (such as when <math>L = X</math> or <math>R \subseteq L</math>) then <math>f(L) \cap f(R) \subseteq f_R</math> if and only if <math>f(R) \subseteq f_R.</math> In particular, taking <math>L = X</math> proves: <math>f(X \setminus R) = f(X) \setminus f(R)</math> if and only if <math>f(R) \subseteq \left\{ y \in f(R \cap X) : f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\},</math> where <math>f(R \cap X) = f(R).</math> <math>\blacksquare</math></ref> 
<math display=block>f(X \setminus R) = f(X) \setminus f(R) \quad \text{ if and only if } \quad f(R) = \left\{ y \in f(R) : f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \right\} \quad \text{ if and only if } \quad f^{-1}(f(R)) \subseteq R.</math>
</li>
<li>If <math>f_R := \left\{y \in f(X) : f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R\right\}</math> then <math>f(X \setminus R) = f(X) \setminus f_R,</math> which can be written more symmetrically as <math>f(X \setminus R) = f_X \setminus f_R</math> (since <math>f_X = f(X)</math>).
</li>
</ul>

=====Formulas for f(L∆R) ={{anchor|Image of symmetric difference|Formulas for the image of symmetric difference}}=====

It follows from <math>L \,\triangle\, R = (L \cup R) \setminus (L \cap R)</math> and the above formulas for the image of a set subtraction that for any function <math>f : X \to Y</math> and any sets <math>L</math> and <math>R,</math>
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f(L \,\triangle\, R)
&= Y ~~~\;~~~\;~~~\; \setminus \left\{ y \in Y ~~~\,~~~\;~~~\,~   ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) = R \cap f^{-1}(y)\right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= f(L \cup R) \setminus \left\{ y \in f(L \cup R)        ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) = R \cap f^{-1}(y)\right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= f(L \cup R) \setminus \left\{ y \in f(L \cap R)        ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) = R \cap f^{-1}(y)\right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= f(L \cup R) \setminus \left\{ y \in V ~~~\,~~~~~~~~~   ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) = R \cap f^{-1}(y)\right\} \qquad && \text{ for any superset } \quad V \supseteq f(L \cap R) \\[0.4ex]
&= f(S) ~~\,~~~\,~\, \setminus \left\{ y \in f(S) ~~~\,~~~\;  ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) = R \cap f^{-1}(y)\right\} \qquad && \text{ for any superset } \quad S \supseteq (L \cup R) \cap X. \\[0.7ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

=====Formulas for f(L) ={{anchor|Image of a set|Formulas for the image of a set}}=====

It follows from the above formulas for the image of a set subtraction that for any function <math>f : X \to Y</math> and any set <math>L,</math><math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f(L)
&= Y ~~~\;\,           \setminus \left\{y \in Y ~~~\;\,           ~:~ f^{-1}(y) \cap L = \varnothing\right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= \operatorname{Im} f \setminus \left\{y \in \operatorname{Im} f ~:~ f^{-1}(y) \cap L = \varnothing\right\} \\[0.4ex]
&= W ~~~\,             \setminus \left\{y \in W ~~\;\,            ~:~ f^{-1}(y) \cap L = \varnothing\right\} \qquad \text{ for any superset } \quad W \supseteq f(L) \\[0.7ex]
\end{alignat}</math>

This is more easily seen as being a consequence of the fact that for any <math>y \in Y,</math> <math>f^{-1}(y) \cap L = \varnothing</math> if and only if <math>y \not\in f(L).</math>

=====Formulas for f(L⋂R) ={{anchor|Image of set intersection|Formulas for the image of set intersection}}=====

It follows from the above formulas for the image of a set that for any function <math>f : X \to Y</math> and any sets <math>L</math> and <math>R,</math>
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f(L \cap R)
&= Y~~~~~ \setminus \left\{y \in Y~~~~~ ~:~ L \cap R \cap f^{-1}(y) = \varnothing\right\}        && \\[0.4ex]
&= f(L)   \setminus \left\{y \in f(L)   ~:~ L \cap R \cap f^{-1}(y) = \varnothing\right\}        && \\[0.4ex]
&= f(L)   \setminus \left\{y \in U~~~~~ ~:~ L \cap R \cap f^{-1}(y) = \varnothing\right\} \qquad && \text{ for any superset } \quad U \supseteq f(L) \\[0.4ex]
&= f(R)   \setminus \left\{y \in f(R)   ~:~ L \cap R \cap f^{-1}(y) = \varnothing\right\}        && \\[0.4ex]
&= f(R)   \setminus \left\{y \in V~~~~~ ~:~ L \cap R \cap f^{-1}(y) = \varnothing\right\} \qquad && \text{ for any superset } \quad V \supseteq f(R) \\[0.4ex]
&= f(L) \cap f(R) \setminus \left\{y \in f(L) \cap f(R) ~:~ L \cap R \cap f^{-1}(y) = \varnothing\right\}        && \\[0.7ex]
\end{alignat}</math>
where moreover, for any <math>y \in Y,</math> 
:<math>L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq L \setminus R~</math> if and only if <math>~L \cap R \cap f^{-1}(y) = \varnothing~</math> if and only if <math>~R \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R \setminus L~</math> if and only if <math>~y \not\in f(L \cap R).</math>
The sets <math>U</math> and <math>V</math> mentioned above could, in particular, be any of the sets <math>f(L \cup R), \;\operatorname{Im} f,</math> or <math>Y,</math> for example.

===(Pre)Images of set operations on (pre)images{{anchor|Images of preimages and preimages of images of set operations}}===

Let <math>L</math> and <math>R</math> be arbitrary sets, <math>f : X \to Y</math> be any map, and let <math>A \subseteq X</math> and <math>C \subseteq Y.</math> 

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Image of preimage
! Preimage of image
! Additional assumptions on sets
|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f\left(f^{-1}(L) \cap R\right) = L \cap f(R)</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=102-120}}

|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f^{-1}(f(L) \cap R) ~\supseteq~ L \cap f^{-1}(R)</math>
|None
|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f\left(f^{-1}(L) \cup R\right) ~=~ (L \cap \operatorname{Im} f) \cup f(R) ~\subseteq~ L \cup f(R)</math>

|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f^{-1}(f(A) \cup R) ~\supseteq~ A \cup f^{-1}(R)</math><ref name="lee-2010-p388">Lee p.388 of Lee, John M. (2010). Introduction to Topological Manifolds, 2nd Ed.</ref><br>
Equality holds if any of the following are true:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f(A) \subseteq R.</math></li>
<li><math>A \subseteq f^{-1}(R).</math></li>
</ol>
|<math>A \subseteq X</math>
|}

'''(Pre)Images of operations on images'''

Since <math>f(L) \setminus f(L \setminus R) ~=~ \left\{y \in f(L \cap R) ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R\right\},</math>

<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f^{-1}(f(L) \setminus f(L \setminus R)) 
&=&& f^{-1}\left(\left\{y \in f(L \cap R) ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R\right\}\right) \\
&=&& \left\{x \in f^{-1}(f(L \cap R)) ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(f(x)) \subseteq R\right\} \\
\end{alignat}</math>

Since <math>f(X) \setminus f(L \setminus R) ~=~ \left\{y \in f(X) ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R\right\},</math>
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f^{-1}(Y \setminus f(L \setminus R)) 
&~=~&& f^{-1}(f(X) \setminus f(L \setminus R)) \\
&=&& f^{-1}\left(\left\{y \in f(X) ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R\right\}\right) \\
&=&& \left\{x \in X ~:~ L \cap f^{-1}(f(x)) \subseteq R\right\} \\
&~=~&& X \setminus f^{-1}(f(L \setminus R)) \\
\end{alignat}</math>

Using <math>L := X,</math> this becomes <math>~f(X) \setminus f(X \setminus R) ~=~ \left\{y \in f(R) ~:~ f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R\right\}~</math> and
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f^{-1}(Y \setminus f(X \setminus R)) 
&~=~&& f^{-1}(f(X) \setminus f(X \setminus R)) \\
&=&& f^{-1}\left(\left\{y \in f(R) ~:~ f^{-1}(y) \subseteq R\right\}\right) \\
&=&& \left\{r \in R \cap X ~:~ f^{-1}(f(r)) \subseteq R\right\} \\
&\subseteq&& R \\
\end{alignat}</math>
and so
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
f^{-1}(Y \setminus f(L)) 
&~=~&& f^{-1}(f(X) \setminus f(L)) \\
&=&& f^{-1}\left(\left\{y \in f(X \setminus L) ~:~ f^{-1}(y) \cap L = \varnothing\right\}\right) \\
&=&& \{x \in X \setminus L ~:~ f(x) \not\in f(L)\} \\
&=&& X \setminus f^{-1}(f(L)) \\
&\subseteq&& X \setminus L \\
\end{alignat}</math>

===(Pre)Images and Cartesian products Π===

Let <math>\prod Y_{\bull} ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \prod_{j \in J} Y_j</math> and for every <math>k \in J,</math> let 
<math display=block>\pi_k ~:~ \prod_{j \in J} Y_j ~\to~ Y_k</math> 
denote the canonical projection onto <math>Y_k.</math> 

'''Definitions'''

Given a collection of maps <math>F_j : X \to Y_j</math> indexed by <math>j \in J,</math> define the map
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
\left(F_j\right)_{j \in J} :\;&& X &&\;\to\;    & \prod_{j \in J} Y_j \\[0.3ex]
                                          && x &&\;\mapsto\;& \left(F_j\left(x_j\right)\right)_{j \in J}, \\
\end{alignat}</math>
which is also denoted by <math>F_{\bull} = \left(F_j\right)_{j \in J}.</math> This is the unique map satisfying 
<math display=block>\pi_j \circ F_{\bull} = F_j \quad \text{ for all } j \in J.</math> 

Conversely, if given a map <math display=block>F ~:~ X ~\to~ \prod_{j \in J} Y_j</math> then <math>F = \left(\pi_j \circ F\right)_{j \in J}.</math>
Explicitly, what this means is that if 
<math display=block>F_k ~\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle\text{def}}{=}~ \pi_k \circ F ~:~ X ~\to~ Y_k</math> 
is defined for every <math>k \in J,</math> then <math>F</math> the unique map satisfying: <math>\pi_j \circ F = F_j</math> for all <math>j \in J;</math> or said more briefly, <math>F = \left(F_j\right)_{j \in J}.</math>

The map <math>F_{\bull} = \left(F_j\right)_{j \in J} ~:~ X ~\to~ \prod_{j \in J} Y_j</math> should not be confused with the [[Cartesian product]] <math>\prod_{j \in J} F_j</math> of these maps, which is by definition is the map 
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{4}
\prod_{j \in J} F_j :\;&& \prod_{j \in J} X          &&~\;\to\;~    & \prod_{j \in J} Y_j \\[0.3ex]
                       && \left(x_j\right)_{j \in J} &&~\;\mapsto\;~& \left(F_j\left(x_j\right)\right)_{j \in J} \\
\end{alignat}</math>
with domain <math>\prod_{j \in J} X = X^J</math> rather than <math>X.</math>

'''Preimage and images of a Cartesian product'''

Suppose <math>F_{\bull} = \left(F_j\right)_{j \in J} ~:~ X ~\to~ \prod_{j \in J} Y_j.</math> 

If <math>A ~\subseteq~ X</math> then
<math display=block>F_{\bull}(A) ~~\;\color{Red}{\subseteq}\color{Black}{}\;~~ \prod_{j \in J} F_j(A).</math> 

If <math>B ~\subseteq~ \prod_{j \in J} Y_j</math> then 
<math display=block>F_{\bull}^{-1}(B) ~~\;\color{Red}{\subseteq}\color{Black}{}\;~~ \bigcap_{j \in J} F_j^{-1}\left(\pi_j(B)\right)</math> 
where equality will hold if <math>B = \prod_{j \in J} \pi_j(B),</math> in which case <math display=inline>F_{\bull}^{-1}(B) = \displaystyle\bigcap_{j \in J} F_j^{-1}\left(\pi_j(B)\right)</math> and 
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>F_{\bull}^{-1}\left(\prod_{j \in J} \pi_j(B)\right) ~=~ \bigcap_{j \in J} F_j^{-1}\left(\pi_j(B)\right).</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 11a}}}}

For equality to hold, it suffices for there to exist a family <math>\left(B_j\right)_{j \in J}</math> of subsets <math>B_j \subseteq Y_j</math> such that <math>B = \prod_{j \in J} B_j,</math> in which case: 
{{NumBlk||<math display=block>F_{\bull}^{-1}\left(\prod_{j \in J} B_j\right) ~=~ \bigcap_{j \in J} F_j^{-1}\left(B_j\right)</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 11b}}}}
and <math>\pi_j(B) = B_j</math> for all <math>j \in J.</math>
