|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f(A) = \varnothing</math> if and only if <math>A = \varnothing</math>

|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f^{-1}(C) = \varnothing</math> if and only if <math>C \subseteq Y \setminus \operatorname{Im} f</math>
|<math>A \subseteq X</math> and <math>C \subseteq Y</math>
|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>L \subseteq R</math> implies <math>f(L) \subseteq f(R)</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=102-120}}

|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>L \subseteq R</math> implies <math>f^{-1}(L) \subseteq f^{-1}(R)</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=102-120}}
|None
|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|The following are equivalent:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f(L) \subseteq f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(L \cup R) = f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap \operatorname{domain} f ~\subseteq~ f^{-1}(f(R))</math></li>
</ol>

|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|The following are equivalent:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f^{-1}(L) \subseteq f^{-1}(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f^{-1}(L \cup R) = f^{-1}(R)</math></li>
<li><math>L \cap \operatorname{Im} f \subseteq R</math></li>
</ol>
If <math>C ~\subseteq~ \operatorname{Im} f</math> then <math>f^{-1}(C) ~\subseteq~ f^{-1}(R)</math> if and only if <math>C ~\subseteq~ R.</math>
|<math>C \subseteq \operatorname{Im} f</math>
|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|The following are equivalent when <math>C \subseteq Y:</math>
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>C \subseteq f(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(B) = C</math> for some <math>B \subseteq R</math></li>
<li>{{nowrap|<math>f(B) = C</math> for some <math>B \subseteq R \cap \operatorname{domain} f</math>}}</li>
</ol>

|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|The following are equivalent:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>L \subseteq f^{-1}(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(L) \subseteq R</math> and <math>L \subseteq \operatorname{domain} f</math></li>
</ol>
The following are equivalent when <math>A \subseteq X:</math>
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>A \subseteq f^{-1}(R)</math></li>
<li><math>f(A) \subseteq R</math></li>
</ol>
|<math>A \subseteq X</math> and <math>C \subseteq Y</math>
|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|The following are equivalent:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f(A) ~\supseteq~ f(X \setminus A)</math></li>
<li><math>f(A) = \operatorname{Im} f</math></li>
</ol>

|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|The following are equivalent:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f^{-1}(C) ~\supseteq~ f^{-1}(Y \setminus C)</math></li>
<li><math>f^{-1}(C) = X</math></li>
</ol>
|<math>A \subseteq X</math> and <math>C \subseteq Y</math>
|-
|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f\left(f^{-1}(L)\right) \subseteq L</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=102-120}}<br>
Equality holds if {{em|and only if}} the following is true:
<ol>
<li><math>L \subseteq \operatorname{Im} f.</math><ref name="halmos-1960-p39">Lee {{harvnb|Halmos|1960|p=39}}</ref><ref name="munkres-2000-p19">Lee {{harvnb|Munkres|2000|p=19}}</ref></li>
</ol>
Equality holds if any of the following are true:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>L \subseteq Y</math> and <math>f : X \to Y</math> is surjective.</li>
</ol>

|style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em 0.5em 1.5em;"|<math>f^{-1}(f(A)) \supseteq A</math><br>
Equality holds if {{em|and only if}} the following is true:
<ol>
<li><math>A</math> is <math>f</math>-saturated.</li>
</ol>
Equality holds if any of the following are true:
<ol style="list-style-type: lower-latin;">
<li><math>f</math> is injective.<ref name="halmos-1960-p39"/><ref name="munkres-2000-p19" /></li>
</ol>
|<math>A \subseteq X</math>
|}

'''Intersection of a set and a (pre)image'''

The following statements are equivalent:
<ol>
<li><math>\varnothing = f(L) \cap R</math></li>
<li><math>\varnothing = L \cap f^{-1}(R)</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=102-120}}</li>
<li><math>\varnothing = f^{-1}(f(L)) \cap f^{-1}(R)</math></li>
<li><math>\varnothing = f^{-1}(f(L) \cap R)</math></li>
</ol>

Thus for any <math>t,</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=102-120}} <math display=block>t \not\in f(L) \quad \text{ if and only if } \quad L \cap f^{-1}(t) = \varnothing.</math>

==Sequences and collections of families of sets==

===Definitions===

A {{em|[[family of sets]]}} or simply a {{em|family}} is a set whose elements are sets.  
A {{em|family over <math>X</math>}} is a family of subsets of <math>X.</math> 

The {{em|[[power set]]}} of a set <math>X</math> is the set of all subsets of <math>X</math>: 
<math display=block>\mathcal{P}(X) ~\colon=~ \{\; S ~:~ S \subseteq X\; \}.</math>

'''Notation for sequences of sets'''

Throughout, <math>S \text{ and } T</math> will be arbitrary sets and <math>S_{\bull}</math> and will denote a [[Net (mathematics)|net]] or a [[sequence]] of sets where if it is a sequence then this will be indicated by either of the notations 
<math display=block>S_{\bull} = \left(S_i\right)_{i=1}^{\infty} \qquad \text{ or } \qquad S_{\bull} = \left(S_i\right)_{i \in \N}</math>
where <math>\N</math> denotes the [[natural numbers]]. 
A notation <math>S_{\bull} = \left(S_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> indicates that <math>S_{\bull}</math> is a [[Net (mathematics)|net]] [[Directed set|directed]] by <math>(I, \leq),</math> which (by definition) is a [[sequence]] if the set <math>I,</math> which is called the net's [[indexing set]], is the natural numbers (that is, if <math>I = \N</math>) and <math>\,\leq\,</math> is the natural order on <math>\N.</math> 

'''Disjoint and monotone sequences of sets'''

If <math>S_i \cap S_j = \varnothing</math> for all distinct indices <math>i \neq j</math> then <math>S_{\bull}</math> is called a {{em|[[pairwise disjoint]]}} or simply a {{em|disjoint}}.  
A sequence or net <math>S_{\bull}</math> of set is called {{em|[[increasing]]}} or {{em|non-decreasing}} if (resp. {{em|[[decreasing]]}} or {{em|[[non-increasing]]}}) if for all indices <math>i \leq j,</math> <math>S_i \subseteq S_j</math> (resp. <math>S_i \supseteq S_j</math>). 
A sequence or net <math>S_{\bull}</math> of set is called {{em|[[strictly increasing]]}} (resp. {{em|[[strictly decreasing]]}}) if it is non-decreasing (resp. is non-increasing) and also <math>S_i \neq S_j</math> for all {{em|distinct}} indices <math>i \text{ and } j.</math> 
It is called {{em|[[Monotone sequence|monotone]]}} if it is non-decreasing or non-increasing and it is called {{em|strictly monotone}} if it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing. 

A sequences or net <math>S_{\bull}</math> is said to {{em|increase to <math>S,</math>}} denoted by <math>S_{\bull} \uparrow S</math>{{sfn|Durrett|2019|pp=1-8}} or <math>S_{\bull} \nearrow S,</math> if <math>S_{\bull}</math> is increasing and the union of all <math>S_i</math> is <math>S;</math> that is, if <math display=block>\bigcup_{n} S_n = S \qquad \text{ and } \qquad S_i \subseteq S_j \quad \text{ whenever } i \leq j.</math>
It is said to {{em|decrease to <math>S,</math>}} denoted by <math>S_{\bull} \downarrow S</math>{{sfn|Durrett|2019|pp=1-8}} or <math>S_{\bull} \searrow S,</math> if <math>S_{\bull}</math> is increasing and the intersection of all <math>S_i</math> is <math>S</math> that is, if <math display=block>\bigcap_{n} S_n = S \qquad \text{ and } \qquad S_i \supseteq S_j \quad \text{ whenever } i \leq j.</math> 

'''Definitions of elementwise operations on families'''

If <math>\mathcal{L} \text{ and } \mathcal{R}</math> are families of sets and if <math>S</math> is any set then define:{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=53-65}}  
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\cup)\; \mathcal{R} ~\colon=~ \{~ L \cup R ~:~ L \in \mathcal{L} ~\text{ and }~ R \in \mathcal{R} ~\}</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\cap)\; \mathcal{R} ~\colon=~ \{~ L \cap R ~:~ L \in \mathcal{L} ~\text{ and }~ R \in \mathcal{R} ~\}</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\setminus)\; \mathcal{R} ~\colon=~ \{~ L \setminus R ~:~ L \in \mathcal{L} ~\text{ and }~ R \in \mathcal{R} ~\}</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\triangle)\; \mathcal{R} ~\colon=~ \{~ L \;\triangle\; R ~:~ L \in \mathcal{L} ~\text{ and }~ R \in \mathcal{R} ~\}</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L}\big\vert_S ~\colon=~ \{ L \cap S ~:~ L \in \mathcal{L} \} = \mathcal{L} \;(\cap)\; \{S\}</math>
which are respectively called '''{{em|elementwise}} {{em|union}}''', '''{{em|elementwise}} {{em|intersection}}''', '''{{em|elementwise}}''' ('''{{em|set}}''') '''{{em|difference}}''', '''{{em|elementwise}} {{em|symmetric difference}}''', and the '''{{em|trace}}'''/'''{{em|restriction of <math>\mathcal{L}</math> to <math>S.</math>}}''' The regular union, intersection, and set difference are all defined as usual and are denoted with their usual notation: <math>\mathcal{L} \cup \mathcal{R}, \mathcal{L} \cap \mathcal{R}, \mathcal{L} \;\triangle\; \mathcal{R},</math> and <math>\mathcal{L} \setminus \mathcal{R},</math> respectively.  
These elementwise operations on families of sets play an important role in, among other subjects, the theory of [[Filter on a set|filters]] and prefilters on sets. 

The {{em|[[Upward closed set|upward closure]] in <math>X</math>}} of a family <math>\mathcal{L} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)</math> is the family: 
<math display=block>\mathcal{L}^{\uparrow X} ~\colon=~ \bigcup_{L \in \mathcal{L}} \{\; S ~:~ L \subseteq S \subseteq X \;\} ~=~ \{\; S \subseteq X ~:~ \text{ there exists } L \in \mathcal{L} \text{ such that } L \subseteq S \;\}</math> 
and the {{em|downward closure of <math>\mathcal{L}</math>}} is the family:
<math display=block>\mathcal{L}^{\downarrow} ~\colon=~ \bigcup_{L \in \mathcal{L}} \mathcal{P}(L) ~=~ \{\; S ~:~ \text{ there exists } L \in \mathcal{L} \text{ such that } S \subseteq L \;\}.</math> 

====Definitions of categories of families of sets====

The following table lists some well-known categories of families of sets having applications in [[general topology]] and [[measure theory]]. 

{{Families of sets|expanded}}

A family <math>\mathcal{L}</math> is called {{em|isotone}}, {{em|ascending}}, or {{em|[[Upward closed set|upward closed]]}} in <math>X</math> if <math>\mathcal{L} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)</math> and <math>\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}^{\uparrow X}.</math>{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=53-65}}  
A family <math>\mathcal{L}</math> is called {{em|downward closed}} if <math>\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}^{\downarrow}.</math>

A family <math>\mathcal{L}</math> is said to be: 
* {{em|closed under finite intersections}} (resp. {{em|closed under finite unions}}) if whenever <math>L, R \in \mathcal{L}</math> then <math>L \cap R \in \mathcal{L}</math> (respectively, <math>L \cup R \in \mathcal{L}</math>). 
* {{em|closed under [[Countable set|countable]] intersections}} (resp. {{em|closed under countable unions}}) if whenever <math>L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots</math> are elements of <math>\mathcal{L}</math> then so is their intersections <math>\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} L_i := L_1 \cap L_2 \cap L_3 \cap \cdots</math> (resp. so is their union <math>\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} L_i := L_1 \cup L_2 \cup L_3 \cup \cdots</math>). 
* {{em|closed under [[Complement (set theory)|complementation]] in}} (or {{em|with respect to}}) {{em|<math>X</math>}} if whenever <math>L \in \mathcal{L}</math> then <math>X \setminus L \in \mathcal{L}.</math> 

A family <math>\mathcal{L}</math> of sets is called a/an: 
* {{em|[[Pi-system|{{pi}}−system]]}} if <math>\mathcal{L} \neq \varnothing</math> and <math>\mathcal{L}</math> is closed under finite-intersections. 
** Every non-empty family <math>\mathcal{L}</math> is contained in a unique smallest (with respect to <math>\subseteq</math>) {{pi}}−system that is denoted by <math>\pi(\mathcal{L})</math> and called {{em|the {{pi}}−system generated by <math>\mathcal{L}.</math>}} 
* {{em|[[filter subbase]]}} and is said to have {{em|the [[finite intersection property]]}} if <math>\mathcal{L} \neq \varnothing</math> and <math>\varnothing \not\in \pi(\mathcal{L}).</math> 
* {{em|[[Filter on a set|filter]] on <math>X</math>}} if <math>\mathcal{L} \neq \varnothing</math> is a family of subsets of <math>X</math> that is a {{pi}}−system, is upward closed in <math>X,</math> and is also {{em|proper}}, which by definition means that it does not contain the empty set as an element. 
* {{em|prefilter}} or {{em|filter base}} if it is a non-empty family of subsets of some set <math>X</math> whose upward closure in <math>X</math> is a filter on <math>X.</math> 
* {{em|[[Field of sets|algebra on <math>X</math>]]}} is a non-empty family of subsets of <math>X</math> that contains the empty set, forms a {{pi}}−system, and is also closed under complementation with respect to <math>X.</math> 
* {{em|[[σ-algebra]] on <math>X</math>}} is an algebra on <math>X</math> that is closed under countable unions (or equivalently, closed under countable intersections).

[[Sequence]]s of sets often arise in [[measure theory]].

'''Algebra of sets'''

{{See also|Algebra of sets|:Category:Properties of binary operations}}

A [[Family of sets|family]] <math>\Phi</math> of subsets of a set <math>X</math> is said to be '''{{em|[[an algebra of sets]]}}''' if <math>\varnothing \in \Phi</math> and for all <math>L, R \in \Phi,</math> all three of the sets <math>X \setminus R, \,L \cap R,</math> and <math>L \cup R</math> are elements of <math>\Phi.</math><ref name="Encyclopedia of math">{{cite web|url=https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Algebra_of_sets|title=Algebra of sets|website=Encyclopediaofmath.org|date=16 August 2013|access-date=8 November 2020}}</ref> 
The [[Algebra of sets|article on this topic]] lists set identities and other relationships these three operations.

Every algebra of sets is also a [[ring of sets]]<ref name="Encyclopedia of math"/> and a [[Pi-system|π-system]]. 

'''Algebra generated by a family of sets'''

Given any family <math>\mathcal{S}</math> of subsets of <math>X,</math> there is a unique smallest<ref group=note>Here "smallest" means relative to subset containment. So if <math>\Phi</math> is any algebra of sets containing <math>\mathcal{S},</math> then <math>\Phi_{\mathcal{S}} \subseteq \Phi.</math></ref> algebra of sets in <math>X</math> containing <math>\mathcal{S}.</math><ref name="Encyclopedia of math"/> 
It is called '''{{em|the algebra generated by <math>\mathcal{S}</math>}}''' and it will be denote it by <math>\Phi_{\mathcal{S}}.</math> 
This algebra can be constructed as follows:<ref name="Encyclopedia of math"/>

<ol>
<li>If <math>\mathcal{S} = \varnothing</math> then <math>\Phi_{\mathcal{S}} = \{\varnothing, X\}</math> and we are done. Alternatively, if <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is empty then <math>\mathcal{S}</math> may be replaced with <math>\{\varnothing\}, \{X\}, \text{ or } \{\varnothing, X\}</math> and continue with the construction.</li>
<li>Let <math>\mathcal{S}_0</math> be the family of all sets in <math>\mathcal{S}</math> together with their complements (taken in <math>X</math>).</li>
<li>Let <math>\mathcal{S}_1</math> be the family of all possible finite intersections of sets in <math>\mathcal{S}_0.</math><ref group=note>Since <math>\mathcal{S} \neq \varnothing,</math> there is some <math>S \in \mathcal{S}_0</math> such that its complement also belongs to <math>\mathcal{S}_0.</math> The intersection of these two sets implies that <math>\varnothing \in \mathcal{S}_1.</math> The union of these two sets is equal to <math>X,</math> which implies that <math>X \in \Phi_{\mathcal{S}}.</math></ref></li>
<li>Then the algebra generated by <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is the set <math>\Phi_{\mathcal{S}}</math> consisting of all possible finite unions of sets in <math>\mathcal{S}_1.</math></li>
</ol>

====Elementwise operations on families====

Let <math>\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{M},</math> and <math>\mathcal{R}</math> be families of sets over <math>X.</math> 
On the left hand sides of the following identities, <math>\mathcal{L}</math> is the {{em|L}}{{hsp}}eft most family, <math>\mathcal{M}</math> is in the {{em|M}}{{hsp}}iddle, and <math>\mathcal{R}</math> is the {{em|R}}{{hsp}}ight most set. 

'''[[Commutative operation|Commutativity]]''':{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=53-65}}  
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\cup)\; \mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R} \;(\cup)\; \mathcal{L}</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\cap)\; \mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R} \;(\cap)\; \mathcal{L}</math>

'''[[Associativity]]''':{{sfn|Császár|1978|pp=53-65}}  
<math display=block>[\mathcal{L} \;(\cup)\; \mathcal{M}] \;(\cup)\; \mathcal{R} = \mathcal{L} \;(\cup)\; [\mathcal{M} \;(\cup)\; \mathcal{R}]</math>
<math display=block>[\mathcal{L} \;(\cap)\; \mathcal{M}] \;(\cap)\; \mathcal{R} = \mathcal{L} \;(\cap)\; [\mathcal{M} \;(\cap)\; \mathcal{R}]</math>

'''Identity''':
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\cup)\; \{\varnothing\} = \mathcal{L}</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\cap)\; \{X\} = \mathcal{L}</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\setminus)\; \{\varnothing\} = \mathcal{L}</math>

'''Domination''':
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\cup)\; \{X\} = \{X\} ~~~~\text{ if } \mathcal{L} \neq \varnothing</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\cap)\; \{\varnothing\} = \{\varnothing\} ~~~~\text{ if } \mathcal{L} \neq \varnothing</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\cup)\; \varnothing = \varnothing</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\cap)\; \varnothing = \varnothing</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{L} \;(\setminus)\; \varnothing = \varnothing</math>
<math display=block>\varnothing \;(\setminus)\; \mathcal{R} = \varnothing</math>

===Power set===

<math display=block>\mathcal{P}(L \cap R) ~=~ \mathcal{P}(L) \cap \mathcal{P}(R)</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{P}(L \cup R) ~=~ \mathcal{P}(L) \ (\cup)\  \mathcal{P}(R) ~\supseteq~ \mathcal{P}(L) \cup \mathcal{P}(R).</math>

If <math>L</math> and <math>R</math> are subsets of a vector space <math>X</math> and if <math>s</math> is a scalar then
<math display=block>\mathcal{P}(s L) ~=~ s \mathcal{P}(L)</math>
<math display=block>\mathcal{P}(L + R) ~\supseteq~ \mathcal{P}(L) + \mathcal{P}(R).</math>

===Sequences of sets===

Suppose that <math>L</math> is any set such that <math>L \supseteq R_i</math> for every index <math>i.</math> 
If <math>R_\bull</math> decreases to <math>R</math> then <math>L \setminus R_\bull := \left(L \setminus R_i\right)_i</math> increases to <math>L \setminus R</math>{{sfn|Durrett|2019|pp=1-8}} 
whereas if instead <math>R_\bull</math> increases to <math>R</math> then <math>L \setminus R_\bull</math> decreases to <math>L \setminus R.</math> 

If <math>L \text{ and } R</math> are arbitrary sets and if <math>L_\bull = \left(L_i\right)_i</math> increases (resp. decreases) to <math>L</math> then <math>\left(L_i \setminus R\right)_i</math> increase (resp. decreases) to <math>L \setminus R.</math> 

====Partitions====

Suppose that <math>S_\bull = \left(S_i\right)_{i = 1}^\infty</math> is any sequence of sets, that <math>S \subseteq \bigcup_i S_i</math> is any subset, and for every index <math>i,</math> let <math>D_i = \left(S_i \cap S\right) \setminus \bigcup_{m=1}^i \left(S_m \cap S\right).</math> 
Then <math>S = \bigcup_i D_i</math> and <math>D_\bull := \left(D_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> is a sequence of pairwise disjoint sets.{{sfn|Durrett|2019|pp=1-8}} 

Suppose that <math>S_\bull = \left(S_i\right)_{i = 1}^\infty</math> is non-decreasing, let <math>S_0 = \varnothing,</math> and let <math>D_i = S_i \setminus S_{i-1}</math> for every <math>i = 1, 2, \ldots.</math> Then <math>\bigcup_i S_i = \bigcup_i D_i</math> and <math>D_\bull = \left(D_i\right)_{i=1}^\infty</math> is a sequence of pairwise disjoint sets.{{sfn|Durrett|2019|pp=1-8}}
